#5490. VantageScore 4.0 can create more homebuyers. Now America needs more homes.

VantageScore 4.0 adds trended credit data and can score more consumers, potentially expanding mortgage eligibility. The article argues added credit access must be paired with zoning and permitting reforms to address a 3.7M to 4.7M housing shortfall.   AI Summary

A credit score should tell lenders not just where a borrower is, but where that borrower is headed.

For example, consider two mortgage applicants who each carry a $5,000 revolving balance today. One paid that balance down from $15,000. The other ran it up from $500. Their current balances are identical, but their trajectory plainly is not.

For decades, mortgages sold to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac relied almost exclusively on a scoring model built largely around a single point-in-time view of credit. That is changing. FHFA approved VantageScore 4.0 and FICO 10T for use by the GSEs in 2022, and in July 2025 announced the interim transition policy allowing VantageScore 4.0 to be used for Enterprise loans. After a limited rollout this spring and summer, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac opened VantageScore 4.0 to every approved lender in September.

The change arrives in a market that remains stubbornly out of reach for many Americans. Rates are well above where they were last decade, prices are near record highs in many markets and inventories are tight. VantageScore 4.0 can help lenders identify creditworthy borrowers who were previously overlooked. But more qualified buyers are only half the equation. Credit availability is not the same as housing availability, and the policy response has to address both.

VantageScore 4.0 incorporates trended credit data: how balances, utilization and repayment behavior have changed over time, rather than a single snapshot. Credit scores have traditionally been very good at taking photographs, but VantageScore 4.0 is instead trying to give lenders a short movie. That is the difference between the two applicants above. Today, VantageScore 4.0 is the only newer trended-data model currently eligible for delivery to the GSEs.

It can also use rent and utility payments when they appear in a consumer’s credit file. For thin-file borrowers with years of on-time payments but little traditional credit, that can be the difference between being scorable and being invisible. The caveat is that on-time rent is still often unreported. VantageScore’s analysis estimates that nearly four million renters could reach a 620 with positive rental data. Wider reporting would unlock more of that.

VantageScore says its model can score up to 33 million more adults than traditional models, and a VantageScore-sponsored analysis identifies nearly five million consumers it considers mortgage-ready.

An Urban Institute analysis of roughly 27.5 million Fannie Mae loans found all three models effective at ranking risk. Both VantageScore 4.0 and FICO 10T captured more defaults in the riskiest decile than Classic FICO, with FICO 10T capturing the most.

That is not a knock on either model. It is the argument for competition. Two modern models pushing each other to become more predictive leave lenders and borrowers better off than a one-model world did.

The market is already moving. In September, Rocket Mortgage said it would make VantageScore 4.0 its preferred model for eligible retail loans starting in the fourth quarter. It made that decision after about four months of testing across 1.4 million credit reports.

Rocket reported that VantageScore helped more clients qualify, and that borrowers who saved money saved an average of about $1,600 at closing. Adoption is still early and concentrated among a few large lenders, but the direction is clear.

VantageScore 4.0 does not replace underwriting. Income, debt-to-income, loan-to-value, reserves, employment stability and collateral still decide who gets a loan. What the model can do is give lenders richer information on a wider pool of borrowers, without asking them to abandon risk discipline.

Implementation matters, too. The two models can assign different scores to the same borrower, and independent analysts have warned that lenders choosing whichever score is higher could introduce bias into default rates. The GSEs have responded with guardrails, including requiring one model across all borrowers on a loan and publishing pricing for each model.

Competition should be judged on predictive accuracy, innovation and cost, not on which model produces the friendliest number on a given file. That is an argument for careful implementation, not for preserving a single-model system.

More qualified buyers means stronger effective demand. Where supply can respond, that demand is a revenue signal that helps marginal projects pencil out. Where zoning, permitting, land and construction costs keep supply frozen, the same purchasing power mostly chases the same homes and shows up in higher prices rather than an inducement for more housing supply.

The scale of the gap is large. Freddie Mac estimates the national housing supply shortfall at about 3.7 million homes, while Zillow puts it at roughly 4.7 million. A separate White House analysis this spring estimated that the United States would have roughly 10 million more single-family homes today if post-2008 construction had continued at historical rates. These measures are not identical, but they point in the same direction: America is not building enough housing.

Supply can respond to better rules. From 2017 to 2022, Minneapolis grew its housing stock 12% while rents rose 1%, according to Pew Charitable Trusts research. Over the same period, the rest of Minnesota grew 4% and saw rents rise 14%. Pew points to reforms including eliminating parking mandates, which made more apartments financially feasible to build.

VantageScore 4.0 can widen the path to homeownership for responsible borrowers, but that path ends at a front door only if there is a home behind it. State legislators and local zoning boards should legalize more housing types, cut parking mandates and shorten permitting timelines. Lenders, scoring companies and policymakers all have a stake in that outcome.

VantageScore 4.0 is a welcome step toward a more competitive, more predictive mortgage credit market. It will hopefully promote America’s needed next step to build more homes for the buyers it helps create.

Kevin C. Gillen, PhD, is Principal Research Fellow with Wilbur C. Henderson Real Estate Institute and Adjunct Professor of Finance at Drexel University. #5489. What I learned sitting on both sides of the REO assignment

A former servicer turned Texas REO broker outlines the habits that improve outcomes, including first 72-hour execution, cash for keys follow-through, defensible BPOs with a plan and proactive communication. The focus is speed, evidence and consistency across long timelines.   AI Summary

I have read an REO assignment from both chairs. For years I sat on the servicer side — short sales at Ocwen, then REO asset management at ShellPoint — deciding which brokers got files, reading their BPOs. Today I run a Texas brokerage that sells bank-owned homes.

I only crossed over in 2021, so the memory is fresh: I run my shop the way I once wished my brokers would run theirs. Good REO outcomes are a team sport; winning teams share a few habits.

The first deliverables come due in 24 to 72 hours, depending on client — no warm-up period. From the asset manager’s chair, the hardest files were rarely the damaged ones. They were the quiet ones: two weeks gone, no occupancy call made — uncertain means occupied, never undecided — the property unsecured, the pre-marketing clock blown: 21 days to listed if vacant, 45 to out if occupied.

The brokers I trusted did the unglamorous work immediately: occupancy confirmed, property secured, condition documented with photos and a first call that said, “Here’s what we’re dealing with.” Ours opens with a pre-marketing review naming every preservation item needed — we don’t wait to be told.

An occupied property is the first fork in the road, and cash for keys is the fastest, cheapest, most humane way through. We average ten to 15 agreements a month, and none of them close themselves. They take follow-up — second and third conversations, not one knock — and thinking outside the box: timing a family’s move, help with logistics, solutions no form anticipates.

Sometimes the right answer sits outside the servicer’s delegation of authority, and it happens when a broker brings a solution and a servicer trusts them enough to flex. That trust, earned file by file, pays for itself in avoided evictions, shorter timelines and properties in better condition.

Every broker has felt the temptation to offer the number that keeps the file; every asset manager felt the hangover when that number meets the market. Price from evidence — photographs, repair scope, listing history — so the asset manager can defend it up the chain, to investors and auditors who never saw the house.

Valuation extends to the details most people walk past: the cleanup, the repairs, the small things that decide the showing — a property put in its best light, with passion for the work.

When an issue surfaces, don’t take it at face value. Investigate it, confirm it’s legitimate, find the solution and solve it fast. And don’t just turn in the BPO: the valuations that stood out came with a marketing plan attached — how the broker would position the property, who the buyer was, what gets cleaned, repaired and photographed before launch.

A number says what a house is worth. A plan says you intend to go get it. That effort goes a long way.

The REO of 20 years ago is not the REO of today. Buyers shop online first, and a bank-owned home competes on the same screen as every listing in its zip code. The standard is the best marketing photos you can produce, virtual staging where warranted and a floorplan. Treating a client’s asset as a second-class listing is a choice — and clients notice who makes it.

In asset management, I didn’t expect perfection; Texas REO will humble anyone. What I couldn’t use was silence. A problem in week one is a task; that problem in week six is a failure.

So we run communication as a system: Once a property is under contract, the asset manager gets a weekly update on it, on schedule, news or not. The brokers I never had to chase were the ones whose updates arrived before I thought to ask.

Two rules cover the rest: If you say you’ll do something, do it — and if you make a mistake, own it plainly and fix it. Never make excuses. Honesty, delivered early and on schedule, is how a client learns they can count on you.

This business is a full-contact sport. Some assignments close in 60 days; some take two years. If you aren’t willing to work a file faithfully for as long as it takes, REO probably isn’t for you. And sometimes helping the client means doing the right thing on a file where there’s nothing in it for you. Do it anyway. That willingness — proven over years, not promised in a pitch — is what turns a vendor into a partner.

Behind every broker an asset manager trusts stands a team: occupancy, preservation, valuations, closings and 100 logistics that never make a report. Managing assets well is a true partnership — broker and team on one side, asset manager and servicer on the other, both pointed at the same goal: the best value for the client.

That means all ten members of my team and our 12 agents, and all the vendors who stand with us in the field — and behind me, my wife and my family. What we’ve achieved in five years rests on their support and on our clients’ trust — the ones who took a chance on me. None of this could be accomplished without everyone believing in me.

I have been the person assigning the file and the person standing in the vacant kitchen at 7 a.m. Both jobs are harder than they look from the other chair — and get easier when the person across the table treats you like a partner. This business doesn’t need disrupting. It needs people who sat in both chairs and remember the view from the other one.

Jonathan Layton is the founder of Luxely Real Estate, a Texas-based brokerage specializing in bank-owned properties.This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. To contact the editor responsible for this piece: [email protected].

#5488. From Bhutan to Zurich: Risk Map 2027 Reveals Where Travelers Are Safest

LUND, Sweden, Nov. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Which countries and cities are among the safest for travelers in 2027, and where are the risks highest? Which countries have become safer over the past year, and which have become riskier? These questions are addressed by the Risk Map 2027, released today by Safeture, a leading provider of People Risk Management technology, and by travel risk intelligence company Riskline.

The map rates countries worldwide on Riskline's five-level scale: Low, Moderate, Medium, High, and Extreme. Risk levels are based on factors such as security, crime, health and environmental risks, and access to medical care. Over the past twelve months, six countries have improved their risk level, and 15 have moved to a higher level.

Ten of the safest and ten of the least safe

For this year's map, Riskline's analysts have selected ten countries and ten cities that stand out as among the safest for travelers, along with ten of each that are among the least safe. The selection spans all global regions and is not a ranking. The destinations are listed alphabetically:

Safe destinations can be found across Europe, Asia, Oceania, and the Americas, from Bhutan and Singapore to Chile, Costa Rica, and Canada. Ottawa is the only city to appear among the safest for the second consecutive year. At the other end of the scale, Kabul, Quetta, Port Moresby, Goma, and Port-au-Prince are again among the least safe cities, joined this year by Bamako, Guayaquil, Sana'a, San Pedro Sula, and Tehran.

Sharpest rise in the Gulf and the wider Middle East

The most striking shift over the past year has occurred in the Middle East. Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates have each moved up two levels, from Moderate to High. Saudi Arabia and Jordan have risen from Medium to High, and Oman from Moderate to Medium. Iran has moved from High to Extreme, the highest level on the scale. For many organizations, these changes matter: the Gulf states are major hubs for business travel, aviation, and regional operations.

Germany and Finland leave the lowest risk level

In Europe, Germany, Finland, and Cyprus have moved from Low to Moderate, as has Greenland. Moderate remains the second-lowest level on the scale, and Europe remains home to several of the map's safest destinations, including Switzerland, Iceland, Slovenia, and Denmark, as well as Oslo, Vienna, Zagreb, and Zurich.

There are also positive developments. Bangladesh, Cameroon, Mozambique, and Nepal have all moved from High to Medium, while El Salvador and the Maldives have improved from Medium to Moderate. Elsewhere, South Sudan has risen from High to Extreme, Guinea-Bissau from Medium to High, and Cuba from Moderate to Medium.

A risk map cannot replace an organization's own risk assessment. Threats describe the situation in a country, while the actual risk depends on the individual traveler: where they are, what they are doing, and how well their organization can support them. As a neutral reference point, the map helps organizations understand the broader landscape, identify emerging patterns, and prepare travelers before they depart.

"This year's map shows how quickly the risk picture can change. Several Gulf states that many companies regard as stable business hubs have moved up two levels in a single year, and even Germany and Finland are no longer at the lowest level. For organizations, the lesson is that duty of care cannot rely on last year's assumptions. It requires up-to-date intelligence and the ability to reach your people quickly," said Jonas Brorson, Chief Marketing Officer at Safeture.

As in previous years, the Risk Map 2027 is free to download at: www.safeture.com/riskmaps

For additional information, visit safeture.com or contact:

Safeture CMO Jonas Brorson: jonas.brorson@safeture.com

About Safeture ABSafeture is a Sweden-based SaaS company that provides a market-leading People Risk Management platform to help organizations protect their people anywhere in the world. By combining real-time risk intelligence, location awareness, and instant mass communication, Safeture enables faster response, stronger duty of care, and better decision-making for global operations. Trusted by medical assistance providers, security companies, insurers, and multinational organizations, Safeture supports travel, facility, and workforce safety through a scalable, partner-centric platform. Safeture AB is listed on Nasdaq First North Growth Market Stockholm (ticker: SFTR). Redeye Nordic Growth AB is the company's Certified Adviser.

About RisklineRiskline is a Denmark-based travel risk intelligence provider and one of the world's leading companies specializing in travel risk analysis. Riskline's professional analysts, supported by artificial intelligence, monitor and process information from more than 100,000 data sources to deliver timely and accurate risk intelligence. Riskline and Safeture have worked together since October 2022.

#5485. IBM, AMD and Oak Ridge join forces to launch quantum computing error-correction platform

IBM Corp., Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and the Quantum Science Center at Oak Ridge National Laboratory today announced a new quantum error-correction platform that integrates quantum and high-performance computing.

Gaining high performance and correctness in quantum computing requires protecting quantum information from noise. In many cases, researchers have paired quantum computers with classical computers to achieve superior performance for running industry-relevant problems. The challenge today is scaling up these advances with classical computing.

Today’s physical quantum qubits make errors roughly once every few hundred operations. Without correction, errors compound rapidly, rendering long or complex calculations completely untenable. Game-changing algorithms such as Shor’s algorithm for factoring or for molecular-scale simulations in chemistry require billions of error-free operations.

This launch uses a co-design platform for quantum error correction using IBM’s quantum computers, including the 120-qubit Nighthawk with ORNL’s Umbra High-Performance Computing system powered by AMD’s Instinct MI355X graphics processing units and 5th Gen EPYC central processing units.

“ORNL’s strength in high-performance computing, combined with the expertise of our QSC partners – like IBM and AMD – creates an opportunity to push the boundaries of what is possible,” said Director of the Quantum Science Center Travis Humble. “With Umbra, we will now test new ideas, evaluate approaches at scale, and build the foundation for more reliable quantum computers.”

Jay Gambetta, an IBM Fellow and director of IBM Research, added that the biggest contributor to today’s research is no longer whether error correction will work on quantum hardware, but how to accelerate and optimize it to build systems scientists can use to tackle problems.

IBM said the Nighthawk’s square-lattice connectivity enables industry-leading speed and real-time control to test error-correction techniques. GPU accelerators, such as AMD’s nodes in the Umbra system, can help with this fine-tuning. The co-design platform connected at Oak Ridge will help explore quantum as part of a broader artificial intelligence and scientific computing infrastructure.

“This new co-design platform for quantum error correction allows us to evaluate different approaches and determine the architectures, software and workflows that will scale,” said Gambetta.

Researchers can measure qubits mid-calculation and act on the results in real time, set the exact timing for the signals that protect the qubits from noise, and see exactly what the hardware ran while working with raw measurement signals. This will provide error-correction research with the raw data needed for the next generation of approaches to build sophisticated capabilities for large systems running real code.

Earlier this year, IBM and ORNL unveiled results showing how workloads running on both quantum and classical computers and the Frontier supercomputer can simulate real magnetic materials and calculate molecular configurations of a promising material for fusion fuel.

The simulation of magnetic materials could lead to breakthroughs in superconductors, more efficient batteries and novel drugs. A promising fusion fuel could provide a stepping stone to abundant energy superior to nuclear fission, which powers current nuclear power plants.

Bitcoin (BTC) might not need another halving, another wave of institutional adoption, or even another round of monetary easing to deliver one of its most explosive rallies yet. Anthropic’s Claude AI predicts that it might need something considerably bigger: a fundamental shift in how the world’s largest economies treat Bitcoin.

Imagine the United States announcing a landmark expansion of its strategic Bitcoin reserve, followed by several major sovereign wealth funds committing billions of dollars to BTC.

Add a deterioration in confidence in traditional government debt and a sudden rush towards alternative stores of value, and Bitcoin could find itself at the center of an extraordinary financial realignment.

The most explosive scenario would begin with Washington committing to actively accumulate Bitcoin rather than simply retaining its existing seized holdings. An official purchasing program, potentially paired with incentives for allied nations to build their own reserves, could fundamentally change Bitcoin’s investment narrative.

The potential domino effect would be enormous:

Government adoption: The US establishes a long-term Bitcoin accumulation strategy, encouraging other nations to follow.

Monetary easing: Deteriorating government debt markets force central banks towards looser monetary policy, potentially increasing demand for scarce assets.

#5481. Exclusive: StrongestLayer launches tools to verify payment requests and block hidden AI instructions

Artificial intelligence email security startup StrongestLayer Inc. today launched two products aimed at email that can move money or manipulate an AI assistant.

The first product, Intent Workflows, can hold payment, payroll and executive account requests for verification before anyone acts on them. Alongside it comes AI Instruction Intercept, which stops hidden instructions in a message before an assistant such as Microsoft Corp.’s Microsoft 365 Copilot reads them

Intent Workflows targets attacks that carry no malware or suspicious link. In vendor email compromise, a criminal takes over a real supplier’s mailbox and sends new bank details inside an existing thread.

StrongestLayer went through 32,052 attacks that got past existing defenses at 45 organizations in the second quarter. Only 3.6% were payment or bank-change requests. Under a loss model built on the Factor Analysis of Information Risk framework, that small slice accounted for more than 98% of the estimated financial exposure. Sender authentication checks were little help, since 94% of those messages passed them.

Traditional email security asks whether a message looks bad, according to Alan LeFort, StrongestLayer’s co-founder and chief executive. “The costliest attacks are built to look fine,” he said. His company looks at what a message is trying to make happen, which for a wire transfer means “verifying the action instead of betting on a verdict.”

StrongestLayer’s detection still screens every message. Intent Workflows adds a hold for the smaller set of requests that can’t be reversed, with each customer deciding whether those requests wait for verification or go to the security team or a process owner.

Customers can also let a request through with a policy banner, which appears only on tracked requests and spells out the company’s own rule, such as “Bank change: call the number on file.” Payments in scope are held whatever the verdict, so a hijacked vendor account can’t get one through by sounding legitimate.

The software compares each payment request with the payee’s history, and customers pick the threshold, whether that is every payment or only those over $5,000. If nothing has changed, the payment owner confirms in one click, in Microsoft Teams or by email. Any change, or a new vendor, means a call to a phone number already on file, and the email isn’t released until the outcome is logged.

Payroll changes are verified the same way, and executive password, multifactor authentication and account recovery resets go to the identity or security team first, even when the request comes in through the help desk.

Eric Sanchez, chief information security officer at law firm Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe LLP, said asking every employee to stay vigilant on every email “has never worked.” Orrick is a StrongestLayer customer and design partner. Under the new setup, every payment that can’t be undone gets “a deliberate check by a named owner,” Sanchez said.

The release also takes on a newer problem. Researchers at Aim Security Ltd. found the EchoLeak flaw in Microsoft 365 Copilot last year, and one crafted email was all it took to get the assistant leaking data.

AI Instruction Intercept reads each message first. A reasoning model checks it for hidden instructions against the customer’s own business context, and only after that does the email reach Copilot, Google LLC’s Gemini or a security classifier. Suspect messages are quarantined by default with an explanation of what each instruction was after.

Email is the one route to an AI assistant that “any outsider can use,” said Joshua Bass, StrongestLayer’s co-founder and chief product officer. He argues the inbox is the first place to stop prompt injection, since all an attacker needs is an address.

Both products are available now for Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace and run alongside a company’s existing email security.

#5480. DT Appoints Daniel Lentz as Chief Financial Officer

Lentz brings 25 years of experience in finance, capital markets, and operations, plus experience as public-company CFO, to drive strategic growth at DT

AUSTIN, Texas, Nov. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- DT (NASDAQ: APPS), the global leader in growth solutions for the mobile ecosystem, today announced the appointment of Daniel Lentz as Chief Financial Officer, effective Nov. 30, 2026. Lentz joins DT at a time of strategic growth, following a reignited mission and brand identity this year, with momentum across its businesses from global engineering and product to scaling data-first solutions and intelligence.

Lentz brings 25 years of experience in finance, capital markets, and operations, plus experience as public-company CFO

Lentz brings 25 years of experience in finance, operations, and investor relations, including public-company work in external financial guidance and capital markets. As Chief Financial Officer, he will lead DT's global finance organization, including all finance functions, legal, and corporate operations.

"Daniel is bringing deep financial, technology, and operational experience to DT," said Bill Stone, Chief Executive Officer, DT. "Combined with his public-company experience, I'm excited by how his skills will accelerate the scalability of our platform, operations, capital markets, and other key financial activities. I also want to thank Josh Kinsell for his service as Interim Chief Financial Officer. Josh will continue as our Chief Accounting Officer, and I'm glad to have his finance expertise alongside Daniel."

Lentz most recently served as Chief Financial Officer and Chief Operating Officer of Commerce.com, a software-as-a-service (SaaS) ecommerce platform. He joined the company in 2018 as Vice President, Finance and Investor Relations, helped lead its initial public offering, drove material improvements to profitability and cash generation, and later oversaw finance, audit, legal, IT, data, and operations.

He also led financial planning at RetailMeNot and spent seven years at Procter & Gamble. Lentz holds an MBA from Cornell University's Johnson Graduate School of Management and a bachelor's degree in finance from the McCombs School of Business at The University of Texas at Austin.

"DT has the reach, the platform, and the momentum, with one billion devices, 82K+ apps, and growth building across key areas of the business," said Daniel Lentz, Chief Financial Officer, DT. "I'm excited to join as DT scales, and I look forward to partnering with the team to turn that into sustained profit growth and strong cash flow, while strengthening the balance sheet and creating long-term value for shareholders."

#5478. Zillow agrees to pay $212.5M to settle investor lawsuit over failed home-flipping business

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 6:40 pmOctober 29, 2026 at 7:46 am

Zillow Group will pay $212.5 million to settle a shareholder class action lawsuit over its handling of Zillow Offers, the home-flipping business it shut down in 2021.

The lawsuit alleged that Zillow executives painted an overly positive picture of Zillow Offers in the months before the shutdown, without disclosing how poorly the company was able to predict home prices. That kept the stock artificially high until Zillow revealed the problems and announced the shutdown in November 2021, according to the complaint.

The Seattle-based company disclosed the settlement Wednesday in an SEC filing. About $48 million of the payment is expected to come from insurance. The deal requires court approval and includes no admission of wrongdoing.

In a statement, a Zillow spokesperson said, “We are pleased that the parties have reached a resolution on the matter.”

The settlement comes about three weeks after the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear Zillow’s challenge to the case’s class status. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce and other business groups backed Zillow’s petition.

Steve Berman, managing partner of Seattle law firm Hagens Berman, the court-appointed class counsel, told Real Estate News he believes it’s the largest single securities settlement in the history of the Western District of Washington, the federal court district that includes Seattle.

Separate shareholder lawsuits filed on the company’s behalf against its leaders, known as derivative suits, remain pending, according to the filing.

Zillow bet its future on buying and selling homes in 2019, when co-founder Rich Barton returned as CEO and projected the business would reach $20 billion in annual revenue within three to five years. The company used its pricing algorithms to buy houses, fix them up and resell them.

The effort unraveled in the fall of 2021. An analyst report found that two-thirds of 650 homes it sampled from Zillow’s inventory were listed for less than the company paid.

Days later, Zillow shut down the business, cut about 2,000 jobs and took a $304 million inventory writedown, with Barton citing the unpredictability of its home-price forecasts. Zillow’s stock fell 32% over two days, according to Reuters.

The original lawsuit, filed that month in federal court in Seattle, cited upbeat statements executives made in the months before the shutdown.

They included a September 2021 remark by Jeremy Wacksman, then Zillow’s chief operating officer and now its CEO, that “the strength and the appeal for Zillow Offers just continues to grow.” Investor Jeremy Jaeger later became the lead plaintiff.

The class covers investors who bought Zillow Class A or Class C shares between Aug. 5 and Nov. 2, 2021. If the judge grants preliminary approval, Zillow will pay the money into a settlement fund within 20 business days.

#5476. Box taps Nvidia’s AI models to build a rich context layer for autonomous enterprise agents

Few technology firms have embraced the arrival of artificial intelligence agents quite like Box Inc., and today it went even further down the road to automation with an expanded partnership with Nvidia Corp.

At its annual customer conference BoxWorks 2026, Box debuted a new retrieval engine that’s powered by Nvidia’s AI models and designed to give AI agents the much-needed context they require to get more work done. It was announced alongside a new orchestration tool for multistep agentic workflows and new threat detection tools designed to safeguard organizations from rogue agents.

Box’s flurry of announcements are designed to fix a growing bottleneck in enterprise AI workflows. As Box Chief Executive Aaron Levie explained, autonomous agents are only as useful as the context they’re fed allows them to be. If AI agents lack context, they’re going to make mistakes, and that means enterprises simply won’t trust them to do any work, stalling adoption.

Levie said that much of the context that AI agents need does not reside in clean, structured databases, but rather deep inside organizations’ messy troves of unstructured data – things such as contracts, software documentation, policy manuals, internal emails, customer communications records and research archives. Companies know that’s the case, but they’re wary about letting autonomous agents jump right into their data. What’s needed is a way to give those agents secure, permission-aware access to this data, so they’re not looking at things they’re not authorized to see or accidentally leaking secrets all over the internet.

This is where Box’s new partnership with Nvidia intends to make a difference. The company today introduced a new tool called Box Content Retrieval, which is a data retrieval engine that transforms messy enterprise content into a structured knowledge base that agents can access more easily and reason over. It was built using Nvidia’s specialized Nemotron Retriever embedding models, which help to create a neat index of unstructured content like scanned documents, images, audio and video files using multimodal and hybrid search techniques.

Box said Box Content Retrieval is able to improve search accuracy by 20% while reducing token consumption by up to 90%, enabling AI agents to find the context they need to improve their response times to worker’s questions by around four-times. It also makes sure that each AI agent adheres to the native file permissions for each piece of content, so they’re never able to access files their users don’t have permission to see.

“By partnering with Nvidia we are creating a new intelligence layer for enterprise content that gives customers faster, more precise ways to ground AI in the content that powers their business,” Levie said.

The new partnership also sees Box bringing Nvidia’s frontier open-weight models to the table, including the new Nemotron 3 Ultra large language model. These models are directly available within Box AI, and because they’re open-weight, they can be accessed at much more affordable prices than proprietary models from companies like Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC.

Nvidia’s open-weight models have been trained on the domain-specific knowledge for highly specialized workflows, Levie said. For instance, financial analysts can use Nemotron Ultra 3 to query loan applications with strict data-access boundaries, while legal teams can use it to identify contract precedents within corporate agreements by understanding their conceptual meaning rather than searching for keyword matches.

“Open weight is an important part of our vision, complementing closed models while driving innovation and broader adoption across the industry,” Levie added.

Holger Mueller of Constellation Research told SiliconANGLE that Box’s partnership with Nvidia bodes well for the company because the chipmaker is by far and away still the world’s leader in AI platforms, and it will allow it to integrate more closely with the leading public cloud providers too. “Documents are a treasure trove for AI in general and context specifically, and enterprises are very keen to tap into them so they can develop better AI applications,” the analyst said. “This confirms the theory that data has to move to the compute in the AI era.”

Box’s AI push isn’t totally reliant on Nvidia. Indeed, it has its own thing going on with Box Architect, a new tool that will launch in beta later this year, allowing business workers to build, test and deploy new agentic processes using their natural language. According to Box, it can connect to native Box tools such as Extract, Automate, Apps and Forms to create complex workflows, with a selection of open and closed models.

Using Box Architect, law firms will be able to build contract review workflows that are informed by their previously-approved playbooks for past agreements, so that they can compare incoming contracts against it. Should it flag any high-risk clauses, these can immediately be sent to an attorney for review. Alternatively, a bank might use Box Architect to build a streamlined client onboarding workflow that collects applications through Forms, verifies identity documents with Extract and then generates and signs an agreement with Doc Gen and Sign.

Deep Analysis analyst Alan Pelz-Sharpe said these are the kinds of coordinated, autonomous workflows that can make a real difference in terms of the value enterprise AI provides. “While legacy approaches require brittle point-to-point configurations for extraction and execution, an integrated agentic design layer dynamically orchestrates content understanding, process steps and analytical visualization within a single governed ecosystem,” he said.

Box also understands that organizations are going to need more security to protect these more advanced and capable AI agents, which is why it’s simultaneously introducing new threat detection capabilities across its platform. The company said the new security tools make it possible to identify the actions of rogue AI agents in real-time, so that if any of them start exfiltrating data in bulk, deleting massive numbers of files, or taking over user accounts, they’ll immediately be flagged for review.

For instance, administrators will be able to control what files each agent can access through classification-based policies, constrain agent’s actions with MCP guardrails that dictate which third-party tools each one can use, and then detect harmful activities that exceed predefined limits.

#5475. Seattle-area startup Group14 raises $169M, plans battery materials factory in Spain

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 29, 2026 at 5:00 amNovember 2, 2026 at 1:32 pm

Next-generation battery materials startup Group14 Technologies today announced $169 million in new funding and plans to build a manufacturing facility in Spain, expanding a production network that includes Washington state and South Korea.

“In order to be a global player in a global industry, we need a global footprint, which means it’s not about picking one specific region and going all in,” Group14 CEO Rick Luebbe told GeekWire. “We really need to grow all regions.”

The startup has developed a silicon-carbon material that replaces graphite in lithium-ion battery anodes, enabling higher energy density and faster charging, according to the company. The material already ships primarily to consumer-electronics customers, while the company pursues automotive and data center applications.

The funding came from a European investor, Luebbe said, but he did not name the firm. It extends the company’s $463 million Series D round and brings Group14’s total funding to nearly $1.5 billion.

The new facility will be located in Sagunto, near Valencia, with production targeted for mid-2029. The site offers clean energy, skilled labor from the chemical industry and proximity to automotive customers, given that Spain is the second-largest vehicle producer in Europe after Germany.

Group14 already has a presence on the continent, acquiring Germany’s Schmid Silicon Technology Holding GmbH in 2023 to secure a European source of silane gas, a key ingredient in its battery material.

Just as the U.S. has been working to bolster its domestic battery manufacturing and reduce its reliance on Chinese supplies, Europe is doing the same, Luebbe said. The company wants to be part of that solution and is eager to make its move.

“Building chemical plants takes a long time, and so you’ve got to think ahead and be able to establish that global footprint and development strategy,” Luebbe said. “We’ve learned a lot in the lifetime of Group14.”

Group14 was founded in 2015 and six years later began operating its first commercial-scale factory, called Battery Active Materials-1, or BAM-1, at its headquarters in Woodinville, Wash.

In 2023, it broke ground on BAM-2 in central Washington’s Moses Lake with funding that included $100 million from the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. The site has two modules that at full capacity will be able to produce up to 4,000 tons of silicon-carbon battery material annually, enough for at least 200,000 electric vehicles.

The company originally aimed to start production by late 2024, a target later pushed to early 2026. Group14 laid off an undisclosed number of Washington workers in July 2025 and furloughed additional employees at Moses Lake in January as it shifted resources toward South Korea. The company’s total headcount is approximately 383 employees.

Luebbe said this week that the company is now targeting mid-2027 to bring the first module online, following equipment installation and commissioning. The second module does not yet have a firm completion date.

“It’s a very complicated infrastructure, and it takes a lot longer than we had anticipated to do the final installation and commissioning,” he added.

The company has at least secured the power it needs. It previously contracted sufficient clean energy to run the site, as well as a planned silane gas facility. Since Group14 began its development, data center deployments have accelerated in the region and projects are competing for clean electricity from hydropower dams.

While BAM-2 has been delayed, Group14’s BAM-3 site in South Korea — which originally began as a joint venture with SK materials — has been producing anode material since 2024. The facility has been scaling up and expects to reach its 2,000-ton annual capacity within about six months.

Group14 is shipping primarily to consumer-electronics customers, which qualify new materials faster than automakers. Luebbe also sees a growing opportunity in data-center battery backup units, where silicon-anode batteries could help smooth rapid spikes in AI-server power demand.

“I’m anticipating data center batteries, battery backup units, to be the second biggest market for us behind EVs,” he said.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5472. Coding Dojo co-founder unveils ‘Idea to Launch,’ a 30-day program to help aspiring founders build with AI

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 29, 2026 at 8:00 amOctober 29, 2026 at 7:47 am

Richard Wang, co-founder and former CEO of coding bootcamp Coding Dojo, is launching Idea to Launch, a 30-day program that helps would-be founders turn a startup idea into a working product using AI coding tools and hands-on engineering help.

Nearly four years after selling Coding Dojo to Perdoceo for $70 million, Wang was looking for a way to keep doing work that had a measurable impact on people’s lives. He found it in mentoring aspiring founders.

Wang thinks AI is about to do for software what smartphones did for video. Cheap cameras and cloud platforms gave rise to the influencer economy, and he believes AI will push the cost of building a product close to zero.

“We’re going to create this whole new builder economy that’s about to come in the next three to five years,” he said. “Baby boomers are gifted with cheap housing. I think Gen Z is going to be gifted with a cheap price to build.”

He sees plenty of demand. Citing a Shopify-Gallup study and a Zapier/Harris poll, Idea to Launch says 60% of Americans have a business idea but only 9% launch one. Wang said the reasons people hold back include fear of failure, not knowing how to get started, and not wanting to give up a paycheck or benefits.

Unlike accelerators such as Techstars or Y Combinator, Idea to Launch doesn’t take equity, and participants don’t have to quit their jobs. Over 10 evening sessions, founders get coaching, run customer interviews, build a product with AI tools such as Lovable, Replit and Cursor, and plan a launch. Each founder also gets 10 hours of one-on-one help from professional engineers.

Wang said people without technical backgrounds can now vibe-code 80% to 90% of a product on their own. The hard part, he said, is connecting it to other services, setting up the database correctly and making it secure.

“We’ll provide that type of knowledge with real engineering support,” he said. For engineers who have never done customer discovery or marketing, the program fills in the business side.

Security researchers have found serious vulnerabilities in apps built on vibe-coding platforms. A 2025 scan found 170 of 1,645 apps built with Lovable exposing user data, and another case this year exposed nearly 19,000 user records. Wang said the program’s engineers will make sure security holes are fixed “before they launch or before they get onto the first customer.”

The first cohort starts Jan. 11, followed by three more through April. Each is capped at 15 to 20 founders. Tuition is $3,500 for the inaugural cohort, down from the normal $5,000. Sessions will be held in person in Seattle or Bellevue, and Wang said he expects to pick a space within the next month. He is self-funding the venture.

Wang, who immigrated from China at 13 and was the first in his family to attend college, became Coding Dojo’s CEO in 2015. He left in 2017 for Trupanion and returned in 2019. The company grew to $50 million in peak annual revenue, according to Wang, and had 194 employees at the time of the sale, according to GeekWire’s earlier reporting. It operated campuses in several states before shifting online during the pandemic.

Wang sees Idea to Launch expanding to other tech hubs, then online, and eventually licensing the program globally, much as Coding Dojo grew to multiple campuses. If the first cohorts go well, he can envision a follow-up program, Launch to Traction, to help founders find more customers.

He doesn’t plan to invest in participants’ companies. Having spent years building and selling Coding Dojo, Wang said he knows how hard that road is and would rather “cheer them on from the sidelines.” He said taking VC money at Coding Dojo created pressure to grow 100% a year, something he calls “startup steroids.”

For Wang, the point isn’t to find the next unicorn. It’s to give more people a shot at building something now that AI has made it cheaper and easier.

“I think everyone should try at least once just to bring their idea to reality,” he said.

#5470. AWS growth hits 39%, its fastest in nearly five years, as Amazon misses on earnings

by Todd Bishop on Oct 29, 2026 at 1:37 pmOctober 30, 2026 at 10:35 am

Amazon Web Services revenue grew 39% to $46 billion in the third quarter, its fastest pace in nearly five years, and Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said he expects the cloud unit to top 40% growth in both 2027 and 2028.

That wasn’t enough for investors. Amazon posted earnings of $1.89 per share, well short of the $1.97 analysts expected, as higher interest costs on its growing debt and other losses ate into its profit.

Operating income beat expectations at $28.1 billion, above the high end of Amazon’s own guidance, and the 13.9% operating margin for the quarter was the highest in the company’s history.

Revenue of $201.9 billion, up 12%, came in just under analyst estimates but at the top of Amazon’s forecast range. Shares fell more than 7% in after-hours trading, after closing down 4% during the regular session.

Update: On the earnings call, Jassy said AWS has a backlog of $578 billion in contracted future revenue, more than double a year earlier. He also said Amazon expects to spend “meaningfully more” on capital projects in 2027 than the roughly $220 billion it plans for this year.

Amazon may need to count on its legendary willingness to be “misunderstood for long periods of time,” as it asks investors to look past the costs to where its biggest businesses are headed.

In the company’s earnings release, Jassy said Amazon’s retail business is gaining market share with improving margins. Retail sales, including online stores, physical stores and third-party seller services, totaled nearly $500 billion over the past 12 months, and AWS is now at a $184 billion annual revenue run rate.

“There has never been a trillion dollar revenue business, and we may have two of them in the next 5-10 years,” he said.

On the earnings call, Jassy said those two businesses are AWS and Amazon’s stores business.

Advertising grew 11% to $19.6 billion, or 12% excluding currency changes, down from 22% on that basis a year earlier. Amazon blamed the timing of Prime Day and a few other factors, and said it expects ad growth to return to the high teens in the fourth quarter.

Online stores grew 2% to $68.5 billion, held back by Prime Day moving into the second quarter this year. Amazon said overall revenue growth would have been about 4 percentage points higher without the shift.

Third-party seller services, the fees Amazon collects from merchants on its site, grew 9% to $46.5 billion. AWS came within about $500 million of it.

Subscription services, which includes Prime memberships, grew 11% to $14 billion.

Physical stores, mostly Whole Foods, grew 2% to $5.7 billion.

Outlook: Amazon expects fourth-quarter revenue of $240 billion to $247 billion, up 12% to 16%, and operating income of $28.5 billion to $33.5 billion.

Amazon CFO Brian Olsavsky said on the earnings call that costs for Amazon Leo, the company’s satellite internet service, are weighing on its fourth-quarter profit forecast as the service gets ready to launch later this year.

Wall Street had expected fourth-quarter operating income of $33.2 billion, near the top of that range, according to analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives. It still expects to spend about $220 billion on capital projects this year.

Amazon’s free cash flow, the cash left over after capital spending, was negative $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with positive $14.8 billion a year earlier, mostly because of its AI investments.

#5468. The Bank of England hiked interest rates and warned inflation could hit around 5%

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The Monetary Policy Committee voted 8-1 to lift the rate to 4%, with one member pushing for a larger 0.5-point increase

The Bank of England raised its key interest rate by 0.25 percentage point to 4% on Thursday as higher energy prices from the conflict in the Middle East push up U.K. inflation, the bank said.

The Monetary Policy Committee voted 8-1 for the increase. Eight members backed a quarter-point rise, while MPC member Catherine L. Mann voted for a half-point increase to 4.25%.

The bank published new forecasts alongside the decision. U.K. CPI inflation rose to 3.5% in September, and the bank expects it to climb to around 5% by the middle of next year. It then projects inflation to ease as the lift that pricier energy gives to annual readings wears off and tight monetary policy keeps weighing on prices.

The move is the bank's first rate increase since August 2023, according to CNBC.

The bank said there is limited evidence of knock-on effects from energy costs on other prices and wages. It judged, however, that "the degree of inflationary pressure in the pipeline is now sufficient to warrant an increase in Bank Rate." Activity data in recent months have generally been stronger than expected, the bank said.

Front-month Brent crude oil futures averaged $108 per barrel over the 15 U.K. working days ending Oct. 27, 38% higher than at the time of the July report.

The bank said monetary policy is not on a pre-set path. The committee will adjust Bank Rate as necessary to return inflation to the 2% target in the medium term.

In the minutes of the meeting, Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey said that "without news which softens the risks to inflationary pressures, I can see the argument for a further increase in rates and thereafter taking a more conditional approach, dependent on the evidence on energy prices and inflation dynamics."

MPC member Alan Taylor, who backed the quarter-point rise, wrote that "this is not the start of a hiking cycle." He described the move as a risk-management "one-for-now" insurance hike.

Mann said research points to non-linear inflation risks. She wrote that "from a risk management and credibility perspective, a 50-basis point hike in Bank Rate is 'good policy.'"

The Bank of England left its key rate unchanged at 3.75% in September, when six committee members voted to hold and three favored a rise to 4%.

The European Central Bank and the Federal Reserve each raised rates by 25 basis points in September, according to the Bank of England's report.

#5466. Emirates saw its profits plunge as the Iran war drives up fuel costs

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The airline's fuel costs before hedging rose 60%, and it carried 22% fewer passengers than a year earlier

Emirates, the airline unit of Emirates Group, reported a 66% drop in profit over the first six months of its fiscal year as regional conflict disrupted its operations and raised jet fuel prices, the company said Thursday.

Emirates' profit after tax for the six months through Sept. 30 was AED 3.3 billion ($903 million). Profit before tax was AED 3.7 billion ($1.0 billion), compared with a record AED 11.4 billion ($3.1 billion) in the same period last year. Revenue fell 13% to AED 56.9 billion ($15.5 billion).

Emirates Group, which includes the services company dnata, posted profit after tax of AED 3.6 billion ($1.0 billion), down 66%. Group revenue fell 12% to AED 66.2 billion ($18.0 billion).

Emirates' fuel bill ahead of hedging climbed 60%, even though its fuel uplift fell 12% on reduced flying. Gains of AED 7.1 billion from its fuel price risk management strategy cut the net increase in fuel costs to 13%. Fuel makes up 34% of the airline's operating costs.

The airline carried 21.8 million passengers, down 22% from a year earlier. Capacity measured in available seat kilometers fell 17%, and the average passenger seat factor was 72.0%, compared with 79.5% a year earlier. At Sept. 30, Emirates was operating 91% of its pre-disruption network.

Cargo revenue rose 52% although tonnage carried fell 1%. The company said the conflict reduced available air freight capacity and pushed shippers toward air freight because of marine transport disruptions.

"It has been a demanding six months," Chairman and Chief Executive Sheikh Ahmed bin Saeed Al Maktoum said in a statement. He said global jet fuel prices doubled from the same period last year, which raised costs and cut profitability. Al Maktoum said the group enters the second half of its financial year with "measured optimism."

The Iran war began Feb. 28 and led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Drones targeted Dubai International Airport in March, according to The Wall Street Journal. The war led Emirates to call off thousands of flights, and the airport halted operations temporarily, according to Bloomberg.

The International Air Transport Association forecast in June that Middle East carriers, including Emirates, would post a collective net loss of $4.3 billion in 2026, reversing a $7.2 billion profit a year earlier, after conflict-related airspace shutdowns disrupted their operations. The trade group projected global airline net profit of $23 billion this year, down from $45 billion in 2025.

#5465. Andy Jassy’s prediction: Amazon could have two $1 trillion businesses within a decade

by Todd Bishop on Oct 29, 2026 at 6:08 pmOctober 31, 2026 at 8:51 am

No company has ever had a business with $1 trillion in annual revenue. Andy Jassy says Amazon is on a path to have two.

Amazon Web Services and the company’s stores business could both reach that milestone in the next five to 10 years, the Amazon CEO said Thursday in the company’s third-quarter earnings release and on its call with analysts.

It’s “pretty rare” for Jassy to make a projection that far out, Morgan Stanley analyst Brian Nowak observed on the call, asking how he gets there.

Jassy’s answer started with AWS, which is at a $184 billion annual revenue run rate after growing 39% in the third quarter. He expects growth of more than 40% in both 2027 and 2028, and pointed to a $578 billion backlog of contracted AWS revenue.

The largest customers reserve capacity in huge blocks, sometimes as much as a gigawatt at a time, giving Amazon “very good visibility” into 2027, 2028 and part of 2029, he said.

Beyond that, he said, businesses are still early in using AI, the cost of running AI models keeps falling, and new uses keep emerging, such as AI models finding and fixing security flaws.

“You can’t predict with any certainty five to 10 years from now, especially at these types of growth rates,” Jassy said of AWS. “But it’s not a stretch for us to imagine that this could be over a trillion dollar business.”

Jassy’s forecast is a big jump from seven months ago. In March, Jassy told employees that AWS had a chance to reach at least $600 billion in annual revenue within about a decade, double his earlier expectation, according to Reuters.

Amazon’s stores business is bigger than AWS. Sales from Amazon’s online and physical stores totaled $309 billion over the past 12 months, or about $575 billion if Jassy is including third-party seller services and advertising in his trillion-dollar projection. We’ve asked Amazon to clarify.

For comparison, Walmart, the world’s largest retailer, had $713 billion in revenue in its most recent fiscal year.

Whichever numbers he’s using, Jassy said “some folks are sleeping a bit” on how much progress the stores business has made.

Jassy argued that Amazon’s stores business is gaining ground on competitors. Amazon added more than $90 billion in gross sales over the past 12 months, he said, and is adding about twice as much per quarter as its next-largest U.S. competitor.

Units sold are up nearly 15% so far this year, Jassy said. He noted that nearly 80% of retail sales still happen in physical stores, which he expects to shift online over time.

The bold prediction came on a rough day for the company. Amazon shares fell more than 7% in after-hours trading after its profit fell short of Wall Street’s expectations.

It’s not going to be cheap to get there. Amazon expects to spend about $220 billion on capital projects this year, mostly for AWS, and Jassy said the company will spend “meaningfully more” in 2027. He said Amazon has “a clear line of sight to attractive financial returns” and is earning back its capital spending faster than before.

The impact is showing up in Amazon’s finances. Its free cash flow, the cash left over after capital spending, was negative $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with positive $14.8 billion a year earlier.

With its spending running ahead of the cash its businesses bring in, Amazon has raised $115 billion through long-term debt this year. Its interest expense more than tripled in the third quarter to $1.7 billion, cutting into its profit.

“We’re in the very early days of this inflection,” Jassy said. “Our strategy is working, and I expect it will for the foreseeable future.”

The company forecast fourth-quarter same-park adjusted EBITDA of $140 million to $150 million, compared with $167 million a year earlier

Six Flags Entertainment forecast fourth-quarter same-park adjusted EBITDA of $140 million to $150 million, versus $167 million in the year-ago period, after a fatal accident at Six Flags Over Georgia and bad weather left October softer than planned. EBITDA stands for earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization.

The company said on Thursday that October fell short of its plan because of unfavorable weather on several of the biggest weekends early in the month, along with the effect of the accident and related ride closures. Six Flags expects about 60 additional operating days in the fourth quarter versus last year, mainly from the return of Holiday in the Park winter events.

“Following the incident at Six Flags Over Georgia last month, we are cooperating fully with the ongoing investigation,” President and Chief Executive Officer John Reilly said in a statement, according to The Wall Street Journal. “We have launched a comprehensive review of ride safety across our entire portfolio, supported by independent third-party engineering and inspection specialists.”

#5462. Power outage takes down KEXP streaming for Seattle radio station’s worldwide audience

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 30, 2026 at 10:23 amNovember 2, 2026 at 8:22 am

KEXP’s website and online streaming were down Friday morning after a power outage hit the Seattle radio station, though its over-the-air broadcast was back and running.

The outage started around midnight, and the station was on and off for a while before it was “knocked offline by a major power outage” between 2 and 3 a.m., said Dashel Schueler, KEXP’s director of marketing and communications. Schueler didn’t know the cause of the outage.

The station’s backup power system, known as an uninterruptible power supply (UPS), also failed.

“There’s no power to the server room infrastructure because the UPS that is supposed to protect all of that gear has failed,” Schueler said. Staff are trying to power critical devices to restore services while they wait for the UPS to be repaired or for a workaround that bypasses it.

There’s no estimate yet for when streaming will return.

Listeners in the Seattle area can tune in at 90.3 FM. The outage affects the KEXP.org stream and the station’s mobile app. KEXP estimates about 175,000 people stream its live broadcast each week, and another 85,000 listen to its shows on-demand.

The outage also took down 92.7 KREV, the station KEXP now owns in the San Francisco Bay Area, which relies on KEXP’s Seattle-based digital infrastructure. Because KEXP’s DJs pick songs live rather than playing a preset playlist, underwriting breaks vary in timing and length, Schueler said. DJs fire the separate Seattle and Bay Area spots manually and at the same time.

KREV was back by around 8:30 to 8:45 a.m., running on a barebones setup KEXP typically uses for remote broadcasts, Schueler said. Listeners may notice some issues while the station gets everything put back together.

Around 7:30 a.m., KEXP DJ John Richards read messages on air from listeners across Seattle who were happy to have the station back — terrestrially at least.

A few posts from listeners on X and Bluesky referenced the streaming outage.

Update: Late Friday afternoon KEXP said it was still working to restore services, but it did manage to put up a temporary livestream on its site.

Update: KEXP CEO Ethan Raup details what went wrong and how it was fixed in this post on LinkedIn.

#5461. Current price of oil as of November 5, 2026

By 6 a.m. Eastern Time today, oil had reached $99.52 per barrel, measured using the Brent benchmark. That’s $6.32 less than it cost yesterday morning and about $35.50 above its price a year earlier.

Oil prices are inherently unpredictable. While many variables come into play, the basic push and pull of supply and demand is what ultimately matters. In times of heightened concern about recession, war, or other major disruptions, oil can swing suddenly.

Each gallon you pay for at the pump bundles together several costs. Crude oil is one piece, but you also pay for refineries, wholesalers, government taxes, and the price markup set by gas stations.

Because crude oil usually accounts for more than half of the price per gallon, it tends to move the needle the most. Sharp increases in oil almost always show up quickly at the pump. Declines in the price of oil, on the other hand, often translate into slower, more delayed drops in gas prices—the “rockets and feathers” effect.

When an emergency arises, the U.S. has a reserve of crude oil called the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its chief function is to secure energy during disasters like sanctions, severe storm damage, or war. It can also help take the edge off brutal price spikes when supply gets hit.

It’s not a solution for the long haul. It’s more of an immediate safety net to support consumers and keep crucial sectors of the economy running (think key industries, emergency services, public transportation, and the like).

Oil and natural gas are two of the main fuels that keep the world running. A big change in oil prices can end up affecting natural gas. As an example, if oil prices increase, some industries may sub natural gas for certain areas of their operations wherever possible. This can increase demand for natural gas.

The oil market typically tracks two benchmarks:

Between the two, Brent offers a clearer view of global oil performance because it prices much of the world’s traded crude. It’s also often the preferred gauge for tracking historical oil trends. In fact, the U.S. Energy Information Administration now uses Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook.

Looking at the Brent benchmark over multiple decades, you’ll find oil has been anything but stable. It’s seen sharp rises due to factors like wars and supply cuts, along with steep declines tied to global recessions and oversupply (called a “glut”). For example:

Bottom line, oil’s historical performance has been anything but smooth. It’s hugely affected by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, evolving energy initiatives and policies, and much more.

Looking to stay up-to-date regarding the latest energy developments? Check out our recent coverage:

The current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic.

The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing.

In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply.

When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf.

#5460. AI agents went shopping for TVs and laptops—and messed up nearly 50% of the time, study shows

As personal AI agents like Muse or Claude become part of daily life, more people are asking them to carry out shopping tasks. But there’s a problem: the agents aren’t very good at shopping. In a first-of-its-kind study, Visa instructed 22 different agents to purchase three everyday items—a TV, a laptop and a hair appliance—and, while some agents did significantly better than others, the overall success rate was only around 57%.

The results of the study are available on a new website by Visa that shows the outcome of 15 separate shopping expeditions by each of the 22 agents. Unsurprisingly, the agents powered by more cutting edge AI models fared best, with the Aragon 4 version of Google’s Gemini and the Wonder version of Meta’s Making notching the highest scores. Both agents made a successful purchase 82% of the time. A Claude agent came in third with a 76% success rate, while an OpenAI agent finished 6th with a 64% success rate.

The diagram below from Visa shows the performance of all 22 models. The vertical axis scores the agents’ success rate, while the horizontal one reflects the cost to run each shopping inquiry. (Visa notes that the five most expensive models succeeded on average 67% of the time, while the cheapest five scored 50%).

The agents’ struggle to make a successful purchase is rooted in part in a simple reality: The motivations behind any given purchase are often complicated and, in many cases, consumers lack information and are not certain what they want.

Visa’s experiment sought to capture this reality by, in the case of TV shoppers, assigning a list of attributes they needed in a television—for instance, compatibility with a child’s gaming console, a 30-day return window, and a model with Dolby Vision. As is the case with real world consumers, the purchaser (who in this case was also an agent) would volunteer some information, but not all of it.

The upshot is that, for an AI agent to succeed in Visa’s experiment, it had to interact with the shopper in a way that would elicit the missing information in a reasonable time. Success amounted to buying a TV that matched the shopper’s needs but, in many cases, the agents bought the wrong product, or simply failed to suggest something suitable at all.

“We’re not there yet from a trust or technology perspective. But we’ll soon get into a world where consumers can trust and delegate,” Visa’s Global Head of Growth, Rubail Birwadker, told Fortune.

Birwadker noted that agent-driven shopping is still in its early days, but that it is advancing rapidly. He added that the focus of Visa’s experiment—product discovery—is just one element of this new type of commerce that retailers and AI companies are trying to figure out.

For AI agents to enter the shopping mainstream, companies will also have to sort out smooth and secure payments—a challenge that Visa and its rival Mastercard are already seeking to address by educating merchants and building tools to facilitate so-called agentic commerce.

There are also new and unresolved legal issues when it comes to AI agents going shopping. Most notably, it’s still unclear who should bear the liability when agents make rogue purchases or commit fraud.

According to Birwadker, these questions will get resolved over time in the same way that an earlier generation of consumers and merchants learned to use ecommerce—he added, though, that agent-based shopping is going to be a very different experience than how we shop online today.

In announcing the results of its agent shopping experiment, Visa also rolled out a website that allows consumers to interact with the agents used in its survey.

Jeff John Roberts is the Finance and Crypto editor at Fortune, overseeing coverage of the blockchain and how technology is changing finance.

Peloton Interactive reported a third straight quarter of year-over-year revenue growth for its fiscal first quarter, which ended Sept. 30, as net income rose to $96 million from $14 million a year earlier.

#5458. Metal fabricator NIC Global to cut 103 jobs near Seattle, move production to Eastern Washington

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 30, 2026 at 10:24 amOctober 30, 2026 at 10:25 am

Metal fabricator NIC Global plans to close its Woodinville, Wash., plant, eliminating 103 jobs. Declining business from local customers is prompting the company to shift production primarily to Eastern Washington to meet data center-related growth.

The layoffs are scheduled to begin Jan. 18, 2027, with final departures Aug. 31, 2028, according to a notice filed with the Washington Employment Security Department. Affected jobs include assembly, engineering, quality assurance, metal fabrication specialists, and forklift positions.

The building will be returned to its landlord when the lease ends in September 2028.

“This is a sad day for our company. Woodinville is where NIC was formed — three Seattle-area sheet-metal shops brought together under one roof in 2001 — and the people in that building built the foundation of everything NIC is today,” Troy Wood, company president and CEO, said via email.

The 100,000-square-foot site mostly served energy and medical device customers. Wood said the volume of work at the plant has declined while demand has increased in Eastern Washington for customers building power distribution technology needed by data centers.

“NIC is a supplier of sheet-metal fabrications and assemblies, and in our business, being close to our customers is what keeps us competitive,” Wood said.

While most of the work from Woodinville will go to Spokane, and a smaller portion will go to NIC’s Gallatin, Tenn., facility. The company also has manufacturing in Pullman; Chillicothe, Ohio; and Denton, Texas. The work outside of Washington is focused on the heavy truck sector. The company’s headcount is nearly 600.

Laid-off workers will be encouraged to apply for openings at other plants.

There are smaller fabricators remaining in the Seattle area, including JEMCO Components & Fabrications, which provides precision machining and sheet-metal fabrication for customers in medical, aerospace and defense sectors, and QUAL-FAB serving medical and dental customers.

NIC’s legal and financial headquarters will stay in the Woodinville area, where the company plans a new office for its finance, IT, sales and West Coast support teams.

Wood praised the quality and reliability of the Woodinville employees’ work.

“I am grateful to every one of them,” he said, “and especially to those who chose to stay with us through two and a half years of uncertainty and kept doing their jobs with integrity.”
