#5457. How the Democratic party flipped the House and Senate, in 12 charts

The 2026 midterm race results saw a blue wave that secured a Democrat majority in both the Senate and House of Representatives. They flipped Senate seats in states the party hadn’t won in decades and took back a House that Republicans had controlled since 2023.

But what led to the turnaround that had voters turn out?

The Democratic party needed a net gain of four seats to win back the Senate, and many in the party had seen 2026 as a testing ground.

“What we’re seeing in the early parts of 2026 really puts Democrats in a good position, as long as we don’t screw it up,” Jen O’Malley Dillon, a Democratic campaign strategist, said at a Dartmouth political event in April. “It’s never been more complex to find a way to reach people. We are such a polarized country when it comes to our politics and, and, you know, people are tuning out in a lot of ways and for good reason—because we need to survive.”

In a stunning showing, Democrats flipped seven Senate seats in North Carolina, South Carolina, Texas, Kansas, Iowa, Ohio and Maine.

Several of the wins came in what were once considered Republican strongholds. Kansas hadn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in almost 100 years, and a surge in turnout helped Democrats win across the South.

The Senate control means Democrats have an effective veto over President Donald Trump’s nominees for the rest of his term.

All 435 House seats were on the ballot, and Democrats went in holding 214. The party then went on to flip 25 Republican seats, and CBS estimates the party could reach 259 seats—well above the 218 Republicans held going in.

Wins came in battleground districts in North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Texas, Michigan, New York, Ohio, Kentucky, and Colorado.

Trump wasn’t on the ballot, but many voters treated the election as a referendum on him. Across age demographics, voters said their vote in Congress was to show opposition to Trump about 39% to 60%, while only 7% to 22% said they voted to show support.

The opposition vote was strongest among the youngest voters—60% of 18- to 29-year olds voted with intent to oppose Trump. Voters 65 and older were the most likely to say they were backing Trump (22%), but even that group leaned toward opposition. Trump himself claimed Republicans would have “won IN A LANDSLIDE” if he had been on the ballot, according to his Truth Social post.

Trump went into election day near the bottom of historical presidential approval. His most recent reading on the presidential approval rating sat at 29%, from Oct. 20. That’s the lowest for any president since George W. Bush fell to 25% in October 2008 during the financial crisis.

Democrats won every age group under 65. Voters 18 to 29 backed Democratic House candidates 72% to Republican candidates’ 25%—but they made up only 11% of the electorate. That’s a sharp turn from 2024, when the youngest voters were roughly split between Trump and Kamala Harris.

The bigger gains came from the middle of the voting population. Voters aged 30 to 44 went Democratic 60% to 36%, and voters 45 to 64—the second largest group at 34%—went 51% to 47%. Only voters 65 and older, the largest group at 35%, narrowly favored Republicans 51% to 48%.

Concern about the economy remained a flashpoint among voters. About four in 10 named the economy as the most important issue facing the country—with the highest shares coming from Black voters (50%) and voters aged 30 to 44 (45%).

The issue a voter named as most important was a strong predictor of their vote. About eight in 10 voters who said the state of democracy was the top issue backed the Democratic House candidate, while immigration was the clearest Republican issue—79% of those voters backed the GOP. Both Democrat and Republicans were close to evenly split on the economy.

Many voters perceived that Congress is not doing enough to check Trump’s presidential powers. Among voters who disapprove of Trump, 94% felt that way. Voters who approved of him were divided.

But neither branch has much public trust. In July, only 4% of adults had a great deal of confidence in the people running Congress, and 53% had hardly any.

The executive branch fared slightly better in public perception, but it still had weak support. With both chambers flipping, Democrats now control what Congress investigates—as the majority now gives the party oversight on presidential powers.

The new Senate class includes several historic firsts: Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed will be the first Muslim U.S. senator, Minnesota’s Peggy Flanagan will be the first Native American woman in the Senate, New Hampshire’s Chris Pappas will be the first openly gay man elected to the chamber, Iowa’s Josh Turek will be the first Paralympian senator and South Carolina’s Annie Andrews will be the first woman elected to the Senate from her state.

In Kansas, Adam Hamilton became the state’s first Democratic senator since 1932. And in Texas, James Talarico beat Ken Paxton—ending a 38-year Democrat drought in the state’s Senate seat and overcoming Elon Musk’s $212 million effort.

Wall Street rallied overall following the midterm results. The S&P 500 was up 1.8% Wednesday morning and the DOW gained more than 1,000 points—but companies tied to Trump, Musk, and the AI buildout moved the other way.

Meanwhile, Trump Media fell 11.7%, adding to a 55% loss for the year. Musk had donated heavily to Republicans during the campaign, and both Tesla and SpaceX fell. Data center power providers took some hits as well: Vistra was down 9.6% and Vertiv 8.7%. Defense contractors including Lockheed Martin and L3Harris lost about 4%.

Joshua Hong is a News Fellow at Fortune covering data, AI, cybersecurity, energy, and retail.

#5456. Filing: Chip startup Powerlattice raises $86M to ease AI’s power crunch

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 30, 2026 at 11:30 amOctober 30, 2026 at 3:35 pm

Powerlattice, a Vancouver, Wash.-based startup developing chips that cut the power demands of AI processors, has raised $86 million, according to an SEC filing on Friday.

The new funding is nearly triple the $31 million the company had raised when it emerged from stealth last November with a $25 million Series A led by Playground Global and Celesta Capital. Board members include former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger, a general partner at Playground, and Steve Fu of Celesta. The filing also lists Wen Hsieh, founding managing partner of Matter Venture Partners, as a director.

The filing shows Powerlattice is seeking $111 million, with 18 investors participating so far. It does not name the investors or the round. The company declined to comment.

AI chips are drawing so much electricity and throwing off so much heat that data center operators are running into limits on available power and cooling.

“AI is not constrained by capital, it’s constrained by power,” Gelsinger said last year when Powerlattice announced its Series A.

Powerlattice makes what it calls a power delivery chiplet, a small component that sits inside the processor package. Conventional setups route current over long paths to the processor, wasting energy along the way. The company says shortening that path can cut energy use by more than half and boost performance. Powerlattice said last year it was providing engineering samples for GPUs, CPUs and custom accelerators.

CEO Peng Zou, Gang Ren and Sujith Dermal founded the company in 2023. The three are semiconductor veterans whose backgrounds span Qualcomm, Intel and NUVIA, a startup Qualcomm acquired in 2021. Powerlattice also has offices in Chandler, Ariz.; San Jose, Calif.; and Hsinchu, Taiwan.

Earlier this week, Powerlattice announced it had demonstrated what it calls the industry’s first monolithic integrated voltage regulator chiplet, which packs the controller, power transistors and inductors onto a single piece of silicon.

In the test, the chiplet powered a device Powerlattice built to mimic the fast-shifting electrical loads of next-generation AI accelerators. The company says multiple chiplets can be linked to work as one, letting chip designers match the setup to their processors.

“Breaking through the AI power wall requires us to rethink how power reaches the processor,” Zou said in the announcement.

Frustration is growing among parts of the XRP community, with one investor accusing Ripple of prioritizing its dollar-pegged RLUSD stablecoin ambitions and leaving longtime XRP holders behind. In an emotional appeal, the investor called on the company’s leadership to recognize the community’s years of loyalty and take action to help unlock XRP’s long-anticipated $20 valuation. The message has reignited debate over whether Ripple’s expanding business strategy will ultimately translate into meaningful gains for XRP holders.

In a November 1 post on X directed at Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse and Ripple CTO Emeritus David Schwartz, XRP investor Fabrizio Scudu criticized the company for allegedly prioritizing its Ripple USD (RLUSD) stablecoin and its broader corporate expansion at the expense of XRP holders. Specifically, he accused Ripple of redirecting XRP’s economic and technological potential toward the stablecoin and other enterprise initiatives, arguing that the company was securing its own future while leaving longtime investors behind.

Scudu said the community had stood by Ripple through nearly a decade of negative sentiment, financial uncertainty, and its prolonged legal wrangle. In his view, investors did more than simply purchase a cryptocurrency; they supported the company through a difficult period, with some committing personal savings and staying loyal to the XRP ecosystem.

To Brad Garlinghouse and David Schwartz: A message for your souls by the fireside.When you sit by the fireside of your homes in the evening, enveloped in the peace and warmth of your families, I look upon you and ask you to look into your souls. That sense of peace, that right to…

Scudu accused Ripple’s leadership of securing the company’s future while leaving longtime XRP holders uncertain about their own financial prospects. He urged the executives to acknowledge the community’s loyalty and sacrifices, arguing that investors deserve to benefit from the ecosystem they helped support through years of challenges.

He also called on Ripple to take meaningful action to help XRP reach what he considers its fair market value of $15 to $20 or higher. In his closing appeal, Scudu framed the issue as one of loyalty and accountability, warning that the community’s contributions should not be forgotten as Ripple continues to expand its business operations. “History is watching you, and so is God,” he concluded.

Meanwhile, as criticism over Ripple’s growing RLUSD business continues to surface, CEO Garlinghouse has pushed back against suggestions that the stablecoin is taking priority over XRP. He recently emphasized during the Swell 2026 conference in New York that Ripple remains committed to its native ecosystem token, declaring, “We will never give up on XRP.”

Garlinghouse also described XRP and RLUSD as “very complementary,” arguing that the two assets serve different but interconnected purposes within Ripple’s broader payments strategy. While RLUSD offers the price stability needed for payments and financial transactions, XRP can provide liquidity and facilitate value transfers across the XRP Ledger.

Garlinghouse further reassured the XRP community that Ripple’s business decisions would not come at the expense of XRP. He stressed that the company “will never do something we think is bad for the XRP ecosystem,” reinforcing his position that RLUSD’s growth is not intended to undermine XRP.

Ultimately, the debate goes beyond Ripple’s growing business footprint. What matters to XRP holders like Scudu is whether that expansion will create meaningful demand for the token itself. More partnerships, payment channels, and RLUSD adoption may strengthen Ripple’s ecosystem, but none of these developments guarantees that XRP will capture enough value to reach the investor’s $20 ambition.

Credit: Austin American-Statesman / Hearst Newspapers / Contributor

Zipline announced a $1.5 billion raise on Thursday at a $21.5 billion post-money valuation, and the drone delivery company is adding 300 Walmart $WMT sites under a new multi-year agreement.

Paradigm, WCM Investment Management and Layer Global led the round, the company said. Valor Equity Partners, Fidelity Management & Research Company, Uber $UBER, Tiger Global, J.P. Morgan, ARK Invest and Salesforce $CRM Ventures also took part. Zipline brought in over $600 million in January when it was valued at $7.6 billion, according to Bloomberg.

In October, the median Zipline order arrived 19 minutes after checkout, compared with more than 30 minutes for traditional delivery, the company said.

#5453. Aspen Institute director: Wealth is not a luxury, but three in four U.S. households don’t have enough

Joanna Smith-Ramani is co-executive director of the Aspen Institute Financial Security Program (Aspen FSP), a leading national voice on how to create paths to prosperity for all Americans.

The Aspen Institute Financial Security Program has created the essential wealth metric as a new way to measure not only how much a family needs to pay the bills but also how much they need for full resilience, prosperity, and well-being. Our finding: Only 26% of U.S. households have essential wealth, the milestone at which families hold multiple appreciating assets—like a home and a retirement account—at levels that allow them to comfortably take risks and plan for the future. For a household in its 30s, for example, that means about $120,000 in net worth and six weeks of take-home pay in liquid savings.

The largest chunk of households, however—43%—are stuck in the middle. There, families have net worth sufficient to cover three months of expenses at the federal poverty line, but fall short of the baseline for meaningful resilience and the foundation for growing prosperity.

Practically, this means they don’t have enough to save for a down payment or have to choose between saving for the emergency car repair or contributing toward retirement—the exact kind of activities that build enough wealth for true financial security. Nor does the gap close with age: Just 24% of households ages 50 to 64 reach essential wealth, leaving most approaching retirement without that security. (The estimates of where households fall on the essential wealth path are based on Aspen FSP calculations of savings and wealth data from the 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances.)

What’s more, when families don’t own the assets critical for reaching essential wealth, they are not only more vulnerable to financial shocks, but they’re also missing out on these assets’ compounding gains, which, in recent decades, have far outstripped income growth. That missed opportunity adds up: Between 2000 and 2024, home prices rose about 60% after inflation and the S&P 500’s total return was roughly 200% after inflation, while real median household income rose about 15%.

This reality matters far beyond any one family. When millions of households are using nearly everything they earn to cover the rising costs of basic needs—fuel, food, housing, health care, child care, and other necessities—the whole economy becomes more fragile. A financial shock such as a job loss or medical bill can force families to cut spending, take on debt, and fall further behind. But when families have savings and assets to fall back on, they can recover more quickly without curtailing their choices or derailing their dreams. In this way, financially resilient families are the foundation of a resilient economy.

The essential wealth framework confirms what many of us already know from experience: Wealth is not a luxury. It’s what allows us to invest in our future, seize opportunity, and handle whatever life throws our way. So the metric isn’t simply a new statistic. It gives leaders a way to design programs that help families build wealth and measure whether those efforts are working—because getting this right, at scale, is both possible and necessary.

#5452. Bitcoin Price Slides, Washington’s Political Balance Shifts, Trump’s Crypto Agenda at Risk

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin price fell toward $75,700 as Democrats captured the Senate in the 2026 midterm elections, raising fresh uncertainty over Trump’s crypto agenda. But Bitcoin has now recovered to $77,700 during Asian trading hours, but remained under pressure as Nasdaq futures plunged and investors reassessed Washington’s political balance.

Democrats secured control of the Senate in a sweeping rebuke to President Donald Trump, winning key races in Texas, Ohio, North Carolina, Kansas and South Carolina. The House outcome remained closely contested, with Democrats also making significant gains.

The result threatens to complicate Trump’s push for clearer crypto regulations. Bitcoin price weakness now reflects both market risk aversion and concerns that Congress could delay legislation designed to establish a federal framework for digital assets.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Bitcoin briefly dropped more than $2,000 after early election results pointed toward a Democratic victory, falling from nearly $78,000 to the $75,000 level. Buyers subsequently stepped in, lifting BTC toward $77,700 this morning.

The selloff extended beyond crypto markets. Nasdaq 100 futures dropped as much as 2.3%, while S&P 500 futures fell 1.3% as investors reacted to the possibility of tighter oversight of technology companies and AI infrastructure projects.

BREAKING: The S&P 500 is now on track to open below 7,500 for the first time since July 31st as markets price-in a Democrat victory in both the House and Senate.Nasdaq 100 futures are now down more than -2% tonight. pic.twitter.com/mBbq77a2mG

The dollar also weakened, while the 10-year Treasury yield slipped six basis points to around 4.90%. The moves raised concerns that a Democratic-controlled Congress could limit Trump’s tax and spending agenda, while increasing regulatory scrutiny across several industries.

Bitcoin’s decline followed an already difficult period for digital assets. The king had slipped below $77,000 earlier in the week as technology stocks weakened and investors reduced exposure to riskier assets.

The election adds another source of uncertainty, although Bitcoin’s recovery from its overnight low shows people have not fully abandoned the market.

The biggest crypto-specific concern involves the Digital Asset Market CLARITY Act, which aims to establish clearer rules governing digital assets and divide oversight responsibilities between U.S. regulators.

The legislation failed to advance through a Senate procedural vote in September, falling short of the 60 votes required. Democrats opposed the measure over concerns about ethics provisions and Trump’s crypto-related business interests.

A Democratic-controlled Senate could make the bill’s path more difficult, particularly if lawmakers prioritize stronger safeguards and additional oversight of the crypto industry.

The election also gives Democrats greater power to investigate the administration and examine potential conflicts of interest involving Trump’s digital asset ventures. Congressional scrutiny could intensify even without new legislation.

However, the result does not automatically mean crypto regulation will become more restrictive. Democrats have supported regulatory frameworks for digital assets, but disagree with Republicans over enforcement, consumer protections and safeguards against political conflicts.

The immediate risk is that negotiations become slower and more complicated, leaving crypto firms without the regulatory clarity they have sought.

Bitcoin price direction will likely depend on whether the election-driven selloff spreads into a deeper market correction. A sustained recovery in Nasdaq could help Bitcoin regain momentum, particularly if investors begin treating the election result as a temporary source of uncertainty rather than a lasting threat to risk assets.

On the other hand, continued weakness in technology stocks could pressure BTC and altcoins further. Investors will also watch whether Democrats pursue aggressive investigations or push for substantial changes to crypto legislation.

The political shift could create a more difficult environment for Trump’s crypto agenda during the final two years of his presidency. Yet a divided government may also limit sweeping policy changes from either party.

For now, Bitcoin price remains caught between broader market weakness and uncertainty over U.S. crypto regulation. The election has changed the political landscape, but the next moves in Congress will determine whether the impact becomes a lasting obstacle for the industry.

#5451. Madrona Prize goes to UW research on agents that shrink AI models to run on small chips

by Todd Bishop on Oct 30, 2026 at 3:13 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 11:53 am

A University of Washington project that uses AI agents to squeeze AI models onto tiny devices — such as a solar-powered camera that spots elk in the wild — won the Madrona Prize at the Allen School’s annual Research Showcase on Thursday.

Seattle venture capital firm Madrona has awarded the prize since 2006 to Allen School student projects that combine strong research with commercial potential. The winners were chosen from among the student posters presented at the evening event on the UW campus.

Zhihan Zhang, a PhD student in the Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering, presented the winning project. It tests whether AI agents can do a job that experts now do by hand: shrinking AI models and tuning device software to run on small, low-power chips with tight limits on memory, power and heat.

In the team’s tests, leading AI models failed at the task without feedback from real hardware. The team built a system that let the agent load its work onto real hardware, measure the results and try again. With that feedback, the agent beat human experts within seven rounds.

The researchers used the approach on two real-world projects: an elk-detection camera trap, which needed its vision model shrunk by 250 times, and a wearable device that records children’s speech for child development research.

The team released its benchmark, called Embedded Arena, as open-source code. Allen School faculty members Shwetak Patel, Vikram Iyer, Natasha Jaques and Kurtis Heimerl also worked on the project.

Other collaborators: Alexander Metzger, Jiuyang Lyu, Chun-Cheng Chang, Jiayi Shao, Yujia Liu, Emmanuel Azuh Mensah, Edward Wang and Gregory D. Abowd.

The People’s Choice award went to Keisuke Kamahori for VibeSys, a project that uses AI agents to write custom software for a specific chip and task, then keep improving it, instead of relying on general-purpose tools built for common setups.

Its first application, VibeServe, writes the behind-the-scenes software that takes requests from users and runs them through an AI model. On Amazon’s Trainium2 chips, the software it built handled up to 2.7 times as much work as an existing system. Shihang (Vic) Li and Allen School faculty members Simon Peter and Baris Kasikci also worked on the project.

The first runner-up for the Madrona Prize, Tanush Yadav, presented VideoNet, a test of how well AI models recognize specific actions in video, such as a particular bouldering move or a type of surgical stitch. It covers more than 1,000 actions across 38 fields.

Leading AI models struggle with it compared to ordinary people. Shown three examples, people improved their accuracy by about 14 percentage points, while AI models improved by about 3 percentage points.

Allen School faculty members Ali Farhadi, Hanna Hajishirzi and Ranjay Krishna, and former Allen School faculty member Yejin Choi, now at Stanford University, also worked on the project.

Other collaborators: Mohammadreza Salehi, Jae Sung Park, Vivek Ramanujan and Rohun Tripathi.

The second runner-up, Henry Wong, presented work on securing benchtop DNA synthesizers, machines that let users print synthetic DNA.

His project focuses on protecting the screening software meant to stop someone from printing a dangerous pathogen, and concludes that even perfectly secure hardware wouldn’t fully solve the problem.

Allen School faculty member Jeff Nivala and former Allen School faculty member Tadayoshi Kohno, now at Georgetown University, also worked on the project.

All of the presenters are PhD students in the Allen School.

Correction: An earlier version of this story misidentified Sethu Raman of Madrona in the lead photo caption.

#5450. Nvidia-backed Agility Robotics becomes first U.S. humanoid robot maker to go public

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The company raised about $465 million through a merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI and related financings, including a Foxconn-led investment

Samuel Boivin / NurPhoto via Getty Images

Agility Robotics began trading on Nasdaq $NDAQ on Thursday as the first U.S. publicly listed pure-play humanoid robotics company with active commercial deployments, the company said. Its common stock and warrants are trading under the symbols "AGLT" and "AGLTW" following the completion of its business combination with Churchill Capital Corp XI.

The business combination and related financings raised about $465 million in gross capital before transaction expenses, the company said. The total includes proceeds from a private investment in public equity led by Foxconn and $100 million of equity funding received before closing. The Foxconn-led investment was roughly $201 million, according to Bloomberg. Nvidia $NVDA, Amazon $AMZN and SoftBank Vision Fund 2 are also backers.

Agility said it will use the proceeds to fulfill customer orders, expand commercial deployments, scale production of its Digit robot and advance its robotics and physical AI platform.

The company said Digit 5, its next-generation humanoid robot, has attracted committed multi-year orders worth more than $300 million. The orders are subject to contractual milestones, product features and specifications. Digit 5 was unveiled in September. Early customer access is expected to begin in the first half of 2027, with general availability targeted for the end of 2027.

Digit operates at GXO, Schaeffler and Toyota $TM Motor Manufacturing Canada, the company said. Agility is expanding its partnership with GXO to deploy Digit at two more U.S. logistics facilities in early 2027. At GXO's Georgia site, Digit has moved more than 100,000 totes. AGCO has signed an agreement for a Digit pilot expected to begin in 2027, and Agility has more than 30 prospective customers in its pipeline.

"Becoming a public company gives us access to more resources to help accelerate that progress, bring intelligent robots to more workplaces and help build a future where people and robots accomplish more together," Agility CEO Peggy Johnson said in a statement.

Digit 5 is designed to work in closer proximity to people, the company said. Earlier Digit models could only work while fenced off by protective barriers, according to Bloomberg. Humanoids with legs are harder to anticipate than wheeled machines, which makes them more hazardous to be around.

Johnson told Bloomberg the listing adds pressure “because we are the first out of the gate and will be the company that others are looking to, not only for those metrics but also safety.”

Agility's listing follows that of a Chinese rival. Unitree Robotics went public on Shanghai's STAR Market in August, when its stock closed 460% above its IPO price in its first session. Unitree competes with Tesla $TSLA and Hyundai Motor Group-owned Boston Dynamics.

#5449. Washington governor rips Microsoft over TV ad in leaked audio

by Todd Bishop on Oct 30, 2026 at 5:21 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 6:29 am

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson called out Microsoft for bankrolling a political action committee responsible for a TV ad describing state government as broken, according to newly leaked audio from a Seattle Chamber leadership conference last week.

Remarks at the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce’s Regional Leadership Conference, held at the Suncadia resort near Cle Elum, Wash., are supposed to be off the record. But The Washington Observer, an independent newsletter on state politics, published the audio Friday, saying it was obtained from an unnamed source.

In the audio, Ferguson zeroed in on a line near the start of the ad — that in Washington, “it used to be all you needed was an idea, a dream and the guts to chase it.”

The governor repeated the words “it used to be” for emphasis, in a tone of disbelief.

“What’s up with that?” Ferguson asked the crowd of business and government leaders. “First, does anyone else in this room believe that? I sure as hell don’t.”

“I talk to people every day who have that idea, that dream. They’re chasing it and they’re getting it,” he said. He cited the record $3.5 billion that Seattle-area startups raised in the third quarter, more than triple the same period a year ago, according to PitchBook data.

The Microsoft relationship: Ferguson, who noted that he had worked as a lawyer for Microsoft, said he loves the company and respects what it does. But he seemed especially peeved that the ad ran during the Seattle Seahawks game, where it reached people across the state and those from elsewhere who might want to come here and start a company.

“If we’re partners, partners should treat partners like partners, right?” he said.

He asked the room to imagine him running a multimillion-dollar ad criticizing Microsoft. “You guys would think I lost my mind if I did that,” he said.

Ferguson called Microsoft a key partner and a member of his economic roundtable, and said he works well with the company. “But it works both ways,” he said.

Ferguson acknowledged that the state has problems. “Are there challenges? Sure,” he said. But he said he didn’t think the ad was “helpful for where we all want to go.”

He told the crowd he welcomes constructive feedback, but asked business leaders to think about how they communicate, and to talk up the state’s workforce, economy and startup funding along with its challenges.

“What we have here is so bloody special,” he said.

Ferguson, who took office in January 2025, also reminded the room that he isn’t going anywhere. “I plan on being governor for a long time,” he said, adding that he works with all of them, “Microsoft included.”

The Observer noted that $10 million, roughly what the group has left to spend, would be a good start on a campaign to run someone else for governor in 2028.

The newsletter said it stripped the audio from a video of Ferguson’s remarks, to protect its source. Among those in the audience was Michael Mattmiller, who represents Microsoft in Olympia. He and Ferguson “kinda-sorta hugged it out afterward,” the Observer reported.

Who’s behind the ad: The campaign comes from Washington Needs to Compete, a PAC funded in large part by Microsoft and its current and former executives. The group has raised about $13.8 million, according to state campaign finance records, including more than $5 million directly from Microsoft.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and former CEO Steve Ballmer each gave $250,000, and Vice Chair and President Brad Smith gave more than $500,000. Other backers include T-Mobile, F5, Alaska Airlines and Weyerhaeuser.

Washington Needs to Compete has spent about $3 million so far, according to state records. Most of it has gone to state legislative races, the Observer reported, including more than $700,000 backing Rep. Amy Walen, D-Kirkland, in the 48th District, home to Microsoft’s Redmond headquarters.

The group spent $97,000 to air the ad during the Seahawks’ Oct. 15 Thursday night loss to the Denver Broncos on Prime Video and $130,000 during their Oct. 25 Sunday night win over the Kansas City Chiefs on NBC, according to the Observer.

Microsoft referred GeekWire’s inquiry to the group, which the company described as a growing coalition of more than 60 funders that want to keep the state competitive.

A press representative for the group sent a statement from Nick Streuli, an officer of Washington Needs to Compete. Streuli runs the government relations firm Sundial Advocacy and was previously policy and outreach director for former Gov. Jay Inslee.

“Washington Needs to Compete is committed to our state and wants to see it succeed,” Streuli said in the statement. “Rising costs are making it harder for businesses to invest and grow here. We are starting a conversation about our economic challenges and how to solve them.”

What the ad says: The spot opens with a nod to “inventors in garages,” “mom-and-pop shops down Main Street” and farmers “feeding the world,” before declaring, “In Washington, it used to be all you needed was an idea, a dream and the guts to chase it.”

Then it turns: “But today, Olympia is broken, spending more while you get less.” Jobs are leaving, the ad says, and “it’s harder than ever to afford a home and raise a family.”

It doesn’t name Ferguson or any legislation. It ends by saying Olympia needs to “quit wasting money, fix what’s broken and put Washington families first.”

Taxes and the business climate: Ferguson this year signed a 9.9% tax on household income above $1 million, known as the millionaires tax, which takes effect in 2028 and is projected to raise about $3 billion a year. Initiative 645, which would repeal it, is on the Nov. 3 ballot.

In September, Smith joined former Gov. Chris Gregoire and dozens of regional officials to launch a partnership aimed at reversing the Seattle area’s economic slide. “The warning signs are flashing on our economy,” Smith said at the time.

The region lost nearly 7,000 jobs in 2025, according to the group, and Washington has fallen from 32nd to 47th in CNBC’s ranking of states by cost of doing business since 2017.

In the same CNBC study, Washington ranks 11th overall, up from 14th last year, and fifth for its economy. WalletHub ranks Washington’s economy second in the nation, behind Massachusetts.

Washington’s gross domestic product grew faster than any other state’s in the first quarter of 2026, driven largely by its tech sector, according to federal data released in June.

Long-term plans: On its website, Washington Needs to Compete describes itself as businesses and residents building “a modern, permanent political organization” to support leaders and ideas that “strengthen our economy, improve affordability and expand opportunity,” through elections and public education.

The site lists its top five contributors as Microsoft, T-Mobile, the Washington Coalition for Responsible Taxes and Spending, F5 and Smith.

The group is saving most of its money for future campaigns, the Observer reported.

Updated Nov. 2 with comment from Washington Needs to Compete.

#5448. Americans hate data centers. Tech needs them

Though the midterms have been dubbed “the AI election” and a resounding repudiation of tech, it’s hard to tell what all this practically means.

There’s a whole lot that’s clear, to be sure. The blue wave was massive, and in part that wave traces back to serious anti-tech sentiment, especially around data centers. It’s worth pinning this down clearly: Americans, right now, overwhelmingly hate data centers. A Gallup and UMass Amherst poll from earlier this year said that more than 70% of Americans oppose data center construction, and the Democrats capitalized (Democrats in over 130 federal and gubernatorial races ran anti-tech or anti-data center ads).

Now, consider: Perhaps the greatest open question around Anthropic, on the eve of its historic IPO, is something like “Can they get enough compute, and can they manage the costs of that process?” The wishes of American voters seem to be on a collision course with the answers that Anthropic (and the AI boom) are looking for.

It gets weirder: While this election was roundly viewed as a disavowal of tech, California’s billionaire tax (famously and financially opposed by Sergey Brin) seems likely dead. And while some data center stocks dropped on Wednesday (Tesla and SpaceX shares also saw non-trivial drops), the Dow actually rallied on Democrats’ victories, up 1500 points.

Brin’s possible success in shooting down the billionaire tax in California has proven singular. Famously, Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz were among the most active donors to Republican candidates in these midterms, to the reported tune of more than $100 million. The same was true of Musk, who reportedly donated well over $400 million. This all got a lot of press in the lead-up to the midterms, and rightfully so.

But most of these billionaires were suspiciously quiet on X on Wednesday, at least as of this writing in the afternoon. Musk was notable in sounding off: “Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time.”

To me, for all the questions that remain, what these results prove goes something like this: The American people are exhausted and afraid of the AI boom, and no amount of billionaires yapping on X or funneling millions into the election is changing that.

Where that takes this world of people I cover from here, I don’t know.

#5447. Molson Coors cut its full-year forecast as beer demand stays soft

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The brewer lowered its net sales and earnings forecasts and expects softer industry volumes to continue in the fourth quarter

Molson Coors $TAP Beverage cut its full-year 2026 guidance on Thursday, pointing to how worldwide economic conditions are shaping both brewing-sector demand and shopper habits, together with continued heavy price promotions in the U.K.

The company said it now anticipates a 1% to 2% drop in net sales at constant currency, whereas its earlier forecast called for flat results, plus or minus 1%. It expects underlying earnings per share to fall 16% to 19% from 2025, versus a prior forecast of a decline of 11% to 15%. Underlying income before income taxes is projected to decline 21% to 24%, compared with a prior range of 15% to 18%. Underlying free cash flow is projected at $1.0 billion, plus or minus 10%, down from $1.1 billion, plus or minus 10%.

The outlook assumes that the weaker global beer industry volume trends seen in both the second and third quarters will carry into the final quarter of the year. It also assumes commodity and logistics costs stay elevated, with the impact of Midwest Premium pricing expected to exceed the prior year by approximately $130 million for the full year.

In its third-quarter results, Molson Coors said net sales fell 1.6% to $2.93 billion. Brand volume dropped 4.9%, and financial volume dropped 3.0%. Underlying income before income taxes decreased 17.4% in constant currency to $349.0 million. Underlying diluted earnings per share were $1.46, down 12.6%.

Net income attributable to the company totaled $271.5 million, equal to $1.45 per share, versus a $2.93 billion loss in the year-earlier period. The prior-year quarter was burdened by a $3.65 billion write-down that partly impaired goodwill.

Revenue missed analyst expectations of $2.94 billion, according to The Wall Street Journal. Adjusted earnings per share topped analyst estimates of $1.44.

Americas net sales fell 1.2%, with U.S. brand volume down 5.6% and industry softness in Canada. EMEA and APAC net sales fell 2.7% on lower U.K. volume, which the company attributed to soft market demand and a heightened competitive landscape. Cost of goods sold per hectoliter rose 8.6%, including approximately $30 million tied to Midwest Premium pricing.

"Those pressures weighed on our performance in the quarter and are likely to remain a factor in the near term," Chief Financial Officer Tracey Joubert said in a statement, according to The Wall Street Journal. She said the company has the balance sheet capacity to manage through periods of cost pressure.

President and CEO Rahul Goyal said in a statement that the company believes its strategy is on the right track, but that its outcomes "are not yet scaled enough to offset the headwinds that we experienced in the third quarter."

Molson Coors scheduled an earnings call with analysts and investors for 8:30 a.m. ET on Thursday.

Other brewers have posted weaker beer results. Carlsberg's beer sales contracted 3.5% on an organic basis in the third quarter, and Constellation Brands $STZ' depletions slipped 0.6% in its fiscal second quarter.

#5445. Pfizer promotes its first female CFO as women’s share of top finance jobs slips

Good morning. After three months as Pfizer’s interim CFO, Cecile Guegan has the job permanently.

Pfizer announced on Tuesday that Guegan was named executive vice president and CFO, effective Nov. 1. As CFO, she will oversee corporate finance functions, operations planning and analysis. She brings more than 25 years of pharmaceutical finance experience.

Guegan joined Pfizer through its 2009 acquisition of Wyeth, where she served as CFO for the Asia Pacific and EMEA/Canada businesses. Most recently, she was senior vice president of finance for Pfizer’s Global Biopharmaceuticals business.

Guegan’s appointment comes as women account for a shrinking share of new CFOs globally, while fewer companies are promoting finance chiefs from within.

According to Russell Reynolds Associates’ latest Global CFO Turnover Index, women accounted for 20% of global CFO appointments in the first three quarters of 2026, down from 24% a year earlier and below the eight-year average of 22%. The trend varied by region. In the Americas, women’s share of CFO appointments rose to 21% from 18%, while EMEA held steady at about 26%. The global decline was concentrated in Asia-Pacific.

Meanwhile, CFO turnover reached its highest Q1-Q3 rate in the index’s eight-year history, rising to 15% from 14% a year earlier. The report also found that fewer companies are filling CFO roles internally, making Guegan’s promotion notable on another front.

Health care fared slightly better, with women accounting for 24% of CFO appointments, just above the sector’s eight-year average of 23%.

James Kehoe will step down as CFO of FIS (NYSE: FIS), a financial technology company, effective Nov. 5. Kehoe will serve as a non-executive senior advisor through March. FIS has appointed Alexandra Brooks, EVP and chief accounting officer, as interim CFO. Brooks will continue to serve as chief accounting officer and will work closely with Stephanie Ferris, FIS chief executive officer and president. The company has initiated a search for a permanent CFO, which will consider both internal and external candidates.

Ryan Steines was appointed CFO of Patterson Companies, Inc., a distributor of medical supplies and business solutions, effective Nov. 3. Steines joins Patterson with more than 25 years of finance leadership experience. Before joining Patterson, Steines spent more than two decades at Medtronic in finance leadership roles, where he most recently served as segment CFO for the cardiovascular portfolio, the company's largest business portfolio. In that role, he helped lead a portfolio-wide turnaround focused on accelerating growth and supporting the consolidation of multiple operating units.

The CFA Institute Systemic Risk Council's new report ranks the biggest threats to financial stability. The council, a nonpartisan group of former government officials and financial and legal experts, ranked 13 risks in three tiers based on how immediate they are, how fast they could spread, and whether their damage could be permanent.

The top tier, made up of risks that "can paralyze global critical infrastructure or freeze international capital markets within a matter of hours," includes geopolitical shocks, AI-driven cyberattacks, sudden extreme climate events, and AI-driven investment concentration. On that last risk, the council warns that if AI productivity doesn't meet "massive market expectations," it could set off a wave of credit and equity defaults "much like the serious market disruptions of the dot-com era."

#5444. ConocoPhillips more than doubled its profit as oil prices climbed

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Adjusted earnings rose to $3.27 a share from $1.61 as the oil producer lifted its quarterly dividend 11%

ConocoPhillips $COP reported third-quarter earnings of $4.0 billion, or $3.34 a share, more than double the $1.7 billion, or $1.38 a share, it earned a year earlier.

Adjusted earnings, which exclude special items, were $3.9 billion, or $3.27 a share, compared with $2.0 billion, or $1.61 a share, in the third quarter of 2025. Special items included the reversal of a tax reserve.

The company said the increase came from higher prices, offset in part by lower volumes. Its average realized price was $61.40 per barrel of oil equivalent, up 32% from $46.44 a year earlier.

Adjusted earnings per share topped the $3.05 that analysts polled by FactSet expected, according to The Wall Street Journal. Revenue was $20.06 billion. That exceeded the $18.38 billion that analysts surveyed by Zacks Investment Research projected, according to The Associated Press.

Production totaled 2.302 million barrels of oil equivalent a day, which was 97,000 fewer barrels daily than in the third quarter of 2025. Excluding the effect of completed acquisitions and dispositions, production declined by 40,000 barrels daily, a 2% drop. Growth in the Lower 48 states was outweighed by the effect of the Middle East conflict on Qatar and by higher royalties at Surmont, the company said.

Cash from operations was $7.2 billion. ConocoPhillips spent $3.1 billion on capital expenditures and investments and received $1.6 billion from sales of noncore assets. It returned $3.4 billion to shareholders, made up of $2.4 billion in share repurchases and $1.0 billion in ordinary dividends. The company ended the quarter with $10.4 billion in cash and short-term investments.

ConocoPhillips increased the ordinary dividend it pays each quarter by 11%, to $0.93 a share. The higher payout covers the dividend for the fourth quarter, which will be paid on Dec. 1 to stockholders of record at the close of business on Nov. 16.

"We strengthened our balance sheet and continued progress toward our 45% return of CFO target for 2026, including increasing our ordinary dividend at a top-quartile S&P 500 growth rate," CEO Andy O'Brien said in a statement.

Looking to the fourth quarter, the company expects to produce between 2.32 million and 2.36 million barrels of oil equivalent daily. Full-year capital expenditure and adjusted operating cost guidance is unchanged. ConocoPhillips will hold a conference call at noon ET on Thursday to discuss the results.

#5442. IBM CEO: rationing AI is a slow way to lose

Arvind Krishna is the chairman, president and CEO of IBM. IBM sells the AI operating layer this piece describes, including watsonx and Red Hat, which IBM owns, and helped build the open-source llm-d project cited here.

This year, for the first time, the world will spend more money running AI systems than training them. Training them was a capital bet placed by a handful of companies. Running them is an operating expense, and it lands on everyone’s P&L, every day, for as long as the system is in use. The question for business leaders is no longer whether AI works. It is whether they can afford to run it at scale.

The response so far has been rationing. Pilots cost so little that nobody tracked them. Production costs real money. So, companies are capping tokens, putting spending meters on screens and reserving the most capable models for an approved few. I understand the instinct. I have long argued that the discipline is in picking three or four focused AI projects and funding them properly so they can scale, rather than running a hundred disparate experiments. But that is a decision about where to spend. Rationing is a decision to underfund what you have already chosen. Rationing the most productive technology you have ever put in your people’s hands is a slow way to lose.

Instead, winning the economics of enterprise AI is determined by three questions: What drives the cost? Who sets the price? And what are you actually spending?

First, what drives the cost? The answer is simple: engineering does. AI agents, like the ones writing software, read roughly 600 words for every one they write. And since nearly all of that reading is repetitive, companies are really paying to reread their own documents again and again. The commercial Internet had the same problem. It got affordable not because bandwidth got cheap, but because the industry stopped sending the same data across the network repeatedly. The same fix works for AI. In an open-source project IBM helped build with Red Hat and Google, the system keeps what the AI has already read and sends each request to the machine that already holds it. On our own systems, 98 percent of what the AI needed was already in the cache, so the chips spent their time on new work instead of repeating old work. With caching and other optimizations that let the chips work in parallel, the same hardware handled seven times more work. The software is open source, and any company can use it today. Caching is not the only optimization technique clever engineers will come up with. A collection of them, worked on continuously, is what will bend the AI cost curve.

Second, who sets the price? Every major AI supplier now offers a discount when a customer’s data is reread, and that is welcome. But a discount on someone else’s platform is a price they set and can revise, while the same efficiency built into infrastructure you operate is a cost structure you own. Most AI budgets assume that serious results require the newest model on the newest chips. Neither is true. Highly capable models are now available with open weights, and they can run on infrastructure you control. For a growing share of work, running them there is becoming essential to managing cost. In one recent test on our own systems, IBM ran an open-weight model to power 3,000 AI agents at once. In one of the tasks on that system, designing hardware for quantum error correction, the open model delivered a 52-fold design speedup for $26 in inference costs. A leading proprietary model produced the better design — a 204-fold speedup — for $299, or more than 10 times the cost even with discounts for cached data. The lesson is not that every workload belongs on open models. When you are exploring hundreds of early candidates, the $26 run is the right tool; when you are finalizing the chip, you pay the $299. You should decide which work runs where, and on whose terms. Choosing models that are fit for purpose is another way to bring costs down.

Third, what are you spending? Companies are used to governing technology against units they can count: a server, a license, a seat, a CPU hour. Even variable cloud spending has a legible chain: an application runs, infrastructure is consumed, and the bill rises when more customers show up. AI breaks that chain because it is a probabilistic machine. The same request might cost two cents one time and two dollars the next, because the system took a different route to the same answer. Run that without control, and no one in your company is deciding what the work costs. The machine is. That is why the systems built above the model matter: they make agents more reliable, limit the tools and data they can touch, and keep costs predictable. The goal is not the cheapest token. It is the highest token yield: the most value for every dollar spent.

All three questions land in the same place. Between your data and your models sits an AI operating layer that connects systems never built to speak to each other, governs which people and agents can use which models, and what each may see and do, decides where AI workloads run based on value and economics, and keeps the record a regulator will one day ask for. This layer is where IBM’s capabilities come together for our clients. We ensure that you own that layer, so you own the economics of AI.

The cost of AI is a consequence of how you deploy it and of where the value sits. A great deal of that value sits inside your own company. Roughly four-fifths of enterprise data is unstructured and largely untouched, and it is not on the open internet. It sits in the claims history of an insurer, the underwriting file of a bank, the patient record of a hospital, the telemetry of an aircraft fleet. This data is too large, too regulated and too embedded in systems that cannot pause to be shipped wherever a vendor prefers to process it. So the intelligence has to come to the data. That is as much a matter of sovereignty and security as of cost.

What you actually pay should be decided inside your own company. The frontier labs will keep driving down the cost of their models, but that only sets the floor. If your supplier built the AI operating layer, then it is not a control; it is a meter. Own that layer yourself, and you can afford to run AI at scale. You will be the one bending the AI cost curve.

Lyft $LYFT announced a new Lyft Go membership on Thursday that bundles a DoorDash DashPass subscription with credits riders can spend on rides or delivery orders.

Lyft Go with DashPass costs $9.99 a month or $96 a year, Lyft said. Members earn 8% back in Lyft Credits on rides, from Wait & Save to Lyft Black, and can redeem the credits on Lyft rides or DoorDash orders. Lyft said any rider can browse nearby DoorDash restaurants in the Lyft app on select trips and start an order before the ride ends, with no membership required.

“With Lyft Go, your ride to work or your ride home from the airport can help cover the cost of dinner,” Siddharth Patil, Lyft’s chief rideshare officer, said in a statement.

Rob Edell, DoorDash’s vice president of DashPass, said in a statement that the partnership turns “everyday rides into everyday rewards.”

Lyft and DoorDash have offered discounts on each other’s services since 2024, according to Bloomberg. Uber $UBER One, which also costs $9.99 a month, returns 5% of ride spending as Uber credits and waives delivery fees. Lyft does not run a food delivery service.

Lyft reported record second-quarter gross bookings of $5.50 billion in August. The company said partnerships, including DoorDash and United Airlines, accounted for roughly 30% of North American rideshare volume in the quarter, a record share.

#5440. How the affordability crisis broke the American Dream — the change in the last several generations is real

People across Europe are taking to the streets to express their frustrations over high food prices, unaffordable housing, stagnant wages, and declining public services. Americans are frustrated too, and those same affordability concerns are the top issue in this year’s midterm election. While we’re not in the streets (yet), frustration over affordability here is so severe that it threatens the viability of the American Dream—and potentially America itself.

If the American Dream was a promise made by the nation to its workers—the promise that if you worked hard, then you could achieve economic security—then that promise is broken. America is much less affordable than it was a few generations ago. This is true for everything from dinner at McDonald’s for a family of five—which cost the equivalent of three hours of minimum wage work in 1955, and today costs nearly an entire eight-hour work day—to buying a home—which is less than half as affordable for the average family today compared to 1960.

“Affordability” is the gap between what things cost and what you can afford to spend, yes, but it’s more than that. Affordability is a capacious political term that describes a series of shortfalls: the gap between the ultra-rich and everyone else, the gap between how economists talk about the economy and people’s everyday experiences, the gap between a “poverty wage” and a “livable wage,” the gap between what politicians promise on the campaign trail and what they deliver in office, and the gap between the promise and the reality of achieving the American Dream in the 21st century.

Affordability is the political issue of our time, a crisis that isn’t going to end unless we understand and address all of those gaps. In today’s political discourse “affordability” is another (perhaps less obviously strident) way to say that for a lot of people (maybe most), capitalism feels broken.

How did we get here? Looking at the language we use to talk about the economy offers some clues.

National economic conditions are difficult to generalize because the economy is complex, and information about the economy is hard to synthesize into an easy-to-comprehend narrative. Personal economic conditions are also difficult to generalize because people do not have the exact same economic circumstances—thanks to differences in age, income, debt, savings, family size, housing status, regional cost of living, and expenditures.

That double complexity means that it’s easy to mislead with economic statistics. Financial news often focuses on the performance of stock markets, the cost of gas or eggs, or inflation or unemployment metrics when it attempts to convey the complexities of economic information. But focusing on any one of those factors—or even all of them—still doesn’t tell a complete story. No one of those parts can ever stand for the whole.

Typically, that’s the kind of situation that calls for a metaphor. A metaphor is what 18th-century rhetorical scholars George Campbell and Giambattista Vico, respectively, called “an allegory in miniature” and a “fable in brief.” Metaphors are compact little nuggets of narrative that work by comparison (comparing a known and easily recognizable thing to an unknown or difficult to describe thing). The “metaphors we live by,” explain George Lakoff and Mark Johnson, shape our very thought.

Economists represent their thinking in equations, charts, and graphs that are difficult to translate into paragraphs. Translating those graphs into paragraphs is an act of metaphorical representation—in this case, using words to describe data trends. The most common metaphor used to describe today’s economy is the letter “K,” where “K” stands for the shape of a graph showing how “the rich get richer and the poor get poorer”; how the “U.S. stock market hits new highs,” as an Associated Press headline read on May 26, 2026, as “2 of 3 Americans are cutting back on spending.”

The “rich get richer and the poor get poorer” K-shaped metaphor tells a story that resonates with a lot of Americans’ experience—opinion polls repeatedly find that frustration with the economy is rampant. “Affordability” is the word that captures that K-shaped metaphorical narrative in political discourse.

Affordability is an interesting word because it describes a literal gap (between what things cost and what you can afford) but it also describes a rhetorical gap between the bureaucratic and technical language of professional economists and investors (those who speak about “national economic indicators” or “stock market gains”) and the vernacular language of people who worry about “bills” and “rent” and “utilities” and “prices” and “interest rates”—people who know the ins and outs of “side hustles,” “buy now, pay later,” “food banks,” “pawn shops,” “gig work,” “GoFundMe,” and “payday loans.”

There are terms that attempt to bridge the rhetorical gap: “cost of living” or “making ends meet,” perhaps, but those phrases don’t get at the real thing, which is that K-shaped gap. Affordability in America is a K-shaped story.

Affordability as a political project is about giving Americans—all Americans—the power to choose how (and whether) they spend their money. The rent is too damn high, but so is the healthcare. The rent is too damn high, but so is the childcare. The rent is too damn high, but so are the groceries, the gas, and the utilities. Everything is too damn high, and Americans have no choice but to pay, charge their credit cards, or buy now, pay later—which is to say, Americans have no choice at all. As a political project affordability asks: “Why don’t we have better choices in the land of the free?”

So how can we understand America’s “affordability crisis” and how we talk about the economy? We can define the terms, examine the stats, and tell the stories. But we make sense of the terms, stats, and stories by putting them into a larger context: America’s affordability crisis is a violation of trust, a violation of the bargain of the American Dream.

In the land of the free, Americans feel trapped. In the home of the brave, Americans are frustrated, stressed, and worried. American political leaders have promised repeatedly to make America more affordable and to make the American Dream possible again, but things have steadily gotten worse. America’s affordability problem has fueled outrage, instability, and extremism. In the nation’s 250th year, a lot of Americans feel left behind, and they fear our best days are behind us. The affordability crisis is an existential crisis for America. The affordability issue isn’t just about Americans’ personal finances. It’s a national crisis of broken trust.

Jennifer Mercieca is a historian of American political rhetoric, professor of communication and journalism at Texas A&M University, and a contributing editor at Zócalo Public Square. She is the author, most recently, of Demagogue for President: The Rhetorical Genius of Donald Trump.

This was written for Zócalo Public Square. Read the original article.

#5439. Pope Leo XIV on AI

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 1, 2026 at 10:11 amNovember 1, 2026 at 10:57 am

On Friday, 17 days after his surgery for lung cancer, Pope Leo XIV stood before a room of AI luminaries at the Vatican and delivered a speech on AI. No pope has engaged with AI as seriously, or as deeply, as Leo XIV. The timing shows how much AI matters to him. His remarks were important, on target, and blessedly short: about 740 words, compared with roughly 42,000 in Magnifica Humanitas, the AI encyclical, which I wrote about in May.

“The future of artificial intelligence is not pre-determined.”

I agree with four of his five points. The fifth, a call for international institutions to govern AI, is where we part ways.

First, “the future of artificial intelligence is not pre-determined.” He wants us to ask of AI, “What purpose should it serve?”

Second, “machines are tools, not persons.” Granting AI legal personhood, he warns, risks “leaving those who suffer harm to confront a faceless entity.”

Third, “certain decisions must never be delegated.” Decisions over life, freedom and the use of force have to stay with people, and he urged the states meeting in Geneva in November to “take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.”

Fourth, intelligent technologies “must never become ends in themselves or serve merely the interests of a privileged few.”

Fifth, “What we currently need are institutions capable of putting these principles into practice, particularly effective international institutions that can safeguard the global common good.”

I disagree with the fifth for two reasons.

The first is that the UN, the obvious candidate, has shown a remarkable inability to act. When Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, the Security Council couldn’t even pass a resolution calling for its withdrawal, because Russia holds a veto. Days later, the General Assembly demanded the same withdrawal by a vote of 141-5, and Russia ignored it.

The second is that international institutions are poorly suited to governing a technology that changes every few months. The pope’s own example makes the case. States have discussed autonomous weapons under a UN weapons convention in Geneva since 2014, with a formal expert group since 2016. After 12 years, the review conference that meets Nov. 16-20 will decide whether to begin negotiating a treaty.

“Take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.”

Thousands of AI researchers, me among them, have called for a ban since 2015. There still isn’t one, and I don’t expect Geneva to deliver it. In those same 12 years, AI went from labeling photos to writing software. I suspect real international cooperation on AI won’t come until the major powers face something like the mutually assured destruction that drove nuclear arms control.

Several AI thinkers spoke at the meeting before the pope did.

Max Tegmark of MIT warned against handing decisions to machines, citing tech executives’ predictions that “AI will be in charge, not humans.”

I agree that people have to stay in charge. When AI causes harm, a person chose to deploy it, and that person should answer for it. That’s the pope’s point about the faceless entity. Tegmark and I disagree about a lot (we debated AI risk in September), but not about this.

Stuart Russell of UC Berkeley went further. “We must turn aside from this trajectory before it is too late and pursue other trajectories,” he said, adding that if developers succeed in building machines more capable than humans, “there’s a good chance that every human being will die.”

I don’t share that view, and the pope didn’t go there either. His concerns are autonomous weapons, accountability and who benefits from AI, and those dangers are already here.

Gary Marcus, an NYU cognitive scientist who also spoke, wrote that “Pope Leo XIV is by far the clearest thinker on AI among prominent world leaders.” I agree.

Marcus also wants red lines for open-ended AI agents that “can kind of do anything on the internet.” Red lines are easy to draw and hard to enforce, which brings us back to the fifth point.

Marcus uses GPS navigation to illustrate a better approach. A GPS navigation app is a form of intelligence, he said, but “GPS navigation systems do not hack into Australian government websites.” He was referring to the OpenAI agent that broke into an Australian government Medicare portal in June.

A GPS app’s access to the internet is narrow and restricted. Daniel Khashabi of Johns Hopkins and I call this bounded autonomy. Alignment tries to make an AI agent choose well. Bounded autonomy limits what the agent is allowed to do: how much it can spend, which tools it can use, and which irreversible actions need a person’s sign-off. The company that deploys the agent sets those bounds in software, so nobody has to wait for a treaty.

In May, I wrote that the Pope can talk, but only we can walk. The first point is the one each of us can act on. AI’s future depends on our choices, and we make some of them every day in what we use, buy and build.

Pope Leo leaves for Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on Nov. 6. I wish him safe travels and a full recovery.

#5438. A BMW supplier warned that chip prices are about to get 'mind-boggling'

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Aumovio's interim head of finance said the company expects a gross earnings hit of about €1 billion in 2027 from higher material prices

Aumovio, the German auto supplier spun off from Continental, cautioned on Thursday that chip costs will climb sharply in 2027 because AI data center demand is strengthening chipmakers’ leverage over prices, according to Bloomberg.

Claus Bauer, Aumovio's interim head of finance, told analysts during a conference call that the supply crunch's impact on the auto industry will "explode" in 2027, according to Bloomberg. He said Aumovio anticipates a hit to gross earnings of about €1 billion ($1.1 billion) in 2027, driven by rising costs for materials, chiefly chip inflation.

Data centers are buying up chips in such quantity and at such high prices that automotive customers can't keep up, Bauer said. He called the cost dynamic "mind-boggling."

Bauer estimated that data centers could see the capacity chipmakers allocate to them double, and said that segment has "no price sensitivity whatsoever." Aumovio does not expect much respite from data center demand in 2027, he said, though limits on power generation could eventually slow the buildout.

Aumovio negotiates supplier contracts annually, so pricing can shift substantially whenever a new year begins, according to Bloomberg. The company plans to recoup part of the added costs by raising prices for customers, and to cover the remainder by redesigning products and trimming spending more widely. Aumovio counts BMW, Volkswagen, Ford $F and BYD as clients, and relies on chips in a range of products, including brake systems and vehicle computers.

Aumovio reported third-quarter results on Thursday. Adjusted sales were €4.0 billion, down 12.0% from €4.5 billion a year earlier. The adjusted EBIT margin was 3.5%, compared with 3.4% in the year-earlier quarter.

The company confirmed its 2026 guidance of adjusted sales of €17.0 billion to €17.5 billion and an adjusted EBIT margin of 3.0% to 4.0%. It said it expects higher raw materials prices and increased costs for memory components to weigh on 2026.

Memory makers have issued similar warnings about tight supply. SK Hynix CEO Kwak Noh-jung forecast in July that 2027 will be the worst year for memory supply in the industry's history. Kwak said customer demand would stay above the company's capacity beyond 2030.

Logitech CEO Hanneke Faber said in September that AI demand had made chips scarce. She said she expects little relief over the next year to year and a half.

#5437. Startup uses motion sensors and AI to tell families when an aging parent’s routine changes

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 2, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 2, 2026 at 9:31 am

Thessai, a Bellevue, Wash., startup led by a former Microsoft HoloLens executive, is rolling out a home monitoring system for older adults that flags trouble without cameras, microphones or wearables.

Motion sensors placed around the home feed Thessai’s AI software, which learns a person’s normal patterns over time, such as when they wake up, how often they use the bathroom and how much they move around. The system then sends an alert through a mobile app when something falls outside that baseline: a long stretch of inactivity, unusual movement at night, or a front door opening at 2 a.m.

Founder and CEO Michael Nassirian started the company after his mother-in-law fell at home and was injured. She had a phone and an emergency button within reach but didn’t use them, and she told no one until the next day, when she needed an ambulance.

The family looked for a way to keep tabs on her and found only wearables and cameras, which she refused. So Nassirian bought motion sensors at Home Depot, put them around her home, and wrote software to alert his wife if her mother stopped moving.

Keeping quiet about a fall or health scare is common among older adults, Nassirian said.

“Number one, they say, ‘I’m OK.’ Number two, ‘I don’t want to bother you,’” he said. “And number three, and most important, is embarrassment. They do not want to advertise it.”

Pendants and smartwatches with fall alerts have long been the default, but they only help if people use them. A review of nearly 120 fall-detection studies co-authored by a University of Alberta researcher found that older adults who fall often don’t use their devices to reach a caregiver. Thessai joins a crop of companies pitching camera-free ambient monitoring instead, including Cherish, which makes radar-based sensors, and Butlr, which uses thermal heat detection.

Nassirian spent nearly two decades at Microsoft, working on Office, Windows and later HoloLens, where he was a partner quality architect. Before that, he spent about 14 years at Texas Instruments in test engineering. He has a master’s in biomedical engineering from the University of Texas at Austin, and since leaving Microsoft he has founded and advised several startups, including ARVR Academy and Predictive AI Research.

After relatives started asking for monitoring systems of their own, Nassirian formally founded Thessai in 2024 and has self-funded it so far. The company sells two packages, Basic and Premium, to families with an older relative living alone. Its Enterprise package gives senior-living operators a dashboard for monitoring multiple residences.

The Basic package, which includes motion sensors and a hub that plugs into the home’s Wi-Fi, costs $195 plus a $38 monthly subscription. Premium adds features such as a panic button and two-way voice check-ins through the hub, and costs $249 plus $59 a month. The sensors run on batteries that Nassirian said last at least a year and a half.

Nassirian said independent-living communities have been the strongest market so far. Memory-care facilities already have staff watching residents closely, he said, while independent-living operators are pitching Thessai to renters as a “smart home” feature.

Nassirian said the older adult decides what gets monitored. Through the app, they can switch off sensors in certain rooms, the bathroom for example, and limit tracking to the kitchen and living room. Caregivers can also tune alerts to cut down on noise, so a parent who routinely sleeps late, for example, doesn’t set one off.

Thessai is going after a large and growing market. Older adults overwhelmingly want to stay in their homes (75%) and communities (73%), according to AARP’s 2024 Home and Community Preferences Survey, and households led by people 80 and older are set to double by 2040.

The startup soft-launched in May and has a few hundred customers, split between families and senior-care operators, Nassirian said. Its advisory board includes Chuck Lytle, who founded Bellevue-based senior housing companies Lytle Enterprises and Leisure Care.

Nassirian said the company is also working with the Department of Veterans Affairs on bringing the system to veterans, including in rural areas, with the option to run it on the VA’s own secure network.

Thessai has four employees in the U.S. and seven in Singapore. Nassirian is now looking to raise outside money, mainly to buy hardware in larger volumes and bring down per-unit costs.

Longer term, he wants to do away with the physical sensors altogether and detect movement from a home’s existing Wi-Fi signals, an approach researchers at Harvard and Carnegie Mellon are studying.

“I’m in technology,” he said. “I’m not going to sit still.”
