NEAR Protocol is climbing as the market weighs a major tokenomics overhaul designed to reduce token inflation and ease long-term selling pressure. The NEAR rally follows crypto governance approval of a proposal to lower the network’s annual issuance ceiling from 2.5% to 1.6% over two years.

The proposal, known as HSP-029, passed with overwhelming support from NEAR’s House of Stake. It would gradually reduce the number of new tokens entering circulation, potentially strengthening the supply outlook as the network expands.

NEAR Plans to Take Millions of Tokens Out of Future IssuanceNEAR Protocol's (@NEARProtocol) $NEAR House of Stake has approved a proposal to reduce maximum annual token issuance from 2.5% to 1.6%.The change will roll out gradually over 24 months, reducing the issuance ceiling… pic.twitter.com/pmPOUrWhoI

The move comes as NEAR Protocol seeks to turn its growing ecosystem activity into stronger value for token holders. With issuance cuts, cross-chain infrastructure, and renewed trading interest converging, we are watching if NEAR can sustain its latest breakout.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

The approved proposal would reduce NEAR’s maximum annual issuance rate from 2.5% to 1.6%, with the change phased in over 24 months. According to the proposal, the reduction could prevent 11.8 million NEAR from entering circulation during the first two years. Over six years, the avoided issuance could reach 66.1 million tokens.

At full implementation, daily issuance would fall from roughly 89,500 NEAR to 57,300 NEAR. The network would retain its existing distribution of newly issued tokens, with 90% going to staking participants and 10% allocated to the protocol treasury.

The overhaul also introduces a trade-off for stakers. Gross staking yields could decline from approximately 5.27% to 3.37%, assuming staking participation remains unchanged.

However, the proposal still requires Security Council review, a 90-day grace period, and validator adoption before the changes become binding.

Beyond tokenomics, NEAR Protocol continues developing its chain-signature technology, which allows accounts to interact with external blockchains. NEAR Intents also supports cross-chain swaps, giving the ecosystem another potential source of activity and fee revenue.

The combination of lower issuance and expanding utility is giving NEAR crypto bulls a fresh narrative. However, the market will need to see sustained demand before the supply reduction translates into a lasting price trend.

NEAR Protocol’s cross-chain ambitions arrive as Bitcoin infrastructure projects compete to bring more functionality to the world’s largest cryptocurrency.

Bitcoin Hyper ($HYPER) is positioning itself as a Bitcoin Layer-2 network designed to support faster transactions, lower fees, and smart-contract functionality. Its architecture aims to connect Bitcoin’s security and liquidity with applications typically associated with more flexible blockchain ecosystems.

Bitcoin Hyper has begun rolling out testnet infrastructure, including a wallet and explorer, as it prepares for broader network testing.

Did somebody order a little extra Bitcoin utility? 👀⚡️https://t.co/VNG0P4FWNQ pic.twitter.com/bQAMiOcdUD

While NEAR Protocol is building cross-chain functionality across multiple networks, Bitcoin Hyper is focusing directly on expanding Bitcoin’s role in decentralized finance. This could become important if Bitcoin holders increasingly seek access to applications, trading, and other on-chain opportunities without moving away from BTC-focused infrastructure.

The project is approaching its planned November 26, 2026, launch, with its presale entering the final stretch. Bitcoin Hyper has raised more than $33.2 million, while HYPER is priced at just $0.0136.

The project also offers staking rewards of 35% APY, adding another incentive for early participants ahead of its anticipated token launch.

With the presale scheduled to end on November 26, the approaching launch is becoming a key milestone for HYPER holders watching for exchange listings and ecosystem growth.

NEAR crypto is trading around the $3.80 area, leaving the $4 level as an important near-term hurdle. A sustained move above $4 could strengthen the recovery narrative and open the door toward the $4.30 region. A stronger breakout could bring the $4.50 area into focus, particularly if broader altcoin sentiment improves.

The tokenomics overhaul gives bulls a fundamental catalyst, but traders will also need to see stronger spot demand and improving market momentum.

On the downside, a failure to hold the $3.70–$3.80 area could expose NEAR to another test of support near $3.50. Continued weakness across the broader crypto market would make a sustained recovery more difficult.

For now, NEAR Protocol has a clear catalyst in its issuance reduction proposal, alongside continued development of its cross-chain ecosystem. The next stage of the crypto rally depends on whether buyers can turn the tokenomics story into sustained demand and push NEAR beyond its immediate resistance levels.

#5397. Zillow CEO’s reality check on AI agents: ‘Finding a home isn’t a chore to hand off to a robot’

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 5:41 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 5:54 pm

People will let AI agents cancel subscriptions and book appointments, but most won’t want one to do their house hunting, predicts Zillow Group CEO Jeremy Wacksman.

Wacksman made the case Wednesday afternoon in prepared remarks on Zillow’s quarterly earnings call, addressing a big issue for the online real estate company: whether AI agents will shop on people’s behalf, bypassing sites such as Zillow.

“No one wants an AI agent to watch a movie or play a game for them, because the enjoyment is the point,” he said. “Dreaming and searching for a home is similar. It’s the fun part of the moving process that people want to do.”

Few decisions are as high-stakes as choosing a home, he said. “Finding a home isn’t a chore to hand off to a robot; it’s a milestone people want to live themselves.”

It’s a key issue for Zillow, which makes most of its money from the home-buying process, including fees from partner real estate agents and its mortgage lending business.

That depends on people browsing Zillow’s listings and connecting with those (human) agents and loan officers. An AI agent that does the searching could change those dynamics and potentially cut Zillow out of the process.

The issue has become more pressing with the rise of personal AI agents such as Meta’s Muse, which launched in September and can book travel and make purchases on people’s behalf, among other everyday tasks.

Amazon blocked Muse from shopping on its site less than two weeks after launch, saying it never agreed to let Muse shop there and that the agent doesn’t identify itself. Amazon is also suing Perplexity over the shopping agent in its Comet browser. A federal appeals court in August overturned an injunction Amazon had won in that case.

So far, Wacksman said, Zillow isn’t seeing meaningful traffic from AI platforms. The company has integrated with OpenAI and Google’s Gemini, and is now working with Anthropic. About 80% of its traffic comes directly to Zillow.

For the third quarter, Zillow’s revenue rose 7% to $724 million, short of its own forecast of $745 million to $760 million, as a sharp rise in mortgage rates slowed home sales.

The company posted a $158 million net loss for the quarter, mostly from agreeing to settle a shareholder lawsuit over Zillow Offers, its defunct home-flipping business.

#5396. PancakeSwap's 69% CAKE Emission Cut Would Make CAKE Less Deflationary

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Cutting CAKE emissions by 69% sounds like the most token-friendly move PancakeSwap could make. But run last week's burn figures through "The Flip," and CAKE's net deflation doesn't speed up. It falls by about 30%.

That's the part missing from coverage of the vote, which is currently running about 98% against. Reports have focused on the drop from 22,500 to 7,000 CAKE per day. They haven't covered the burn the proposal removes to fund higher LP payouts. I rebuilt the supply math using PancakeSwap's own weekly burn breakdown. The result is more interesting than a straightforward "cut emissions, good for CAKE" story.

The Flip governance vote is a binary For/Against vote. It opened on October 21 at 08:07 UTC and closes on October 24 at 08:07 UTC. As of Thursday afternoon, the vote page showed:

One address, 0x3D...e1ad, cast 765,559 votes against, about 61% of all voting power used so far.

That share has fallen as more voters joined, and the result would be lopsided even without that wallet. Excluding it, "Against" still has more than 95%. With only 32 votes cast, though, this is mainly a verdict from a small group of large veCAKE holders, not a broad community poll.

The proposal, first posted on PancakeSwap's forum on October 14, has two parts.

Emissions: Daily CAKE emissions would drop from 22,500 to 7,000, with the remaining 7,000 going to a new ecosystem fund called the Pantry. The cut happens in two stages: first to 11,000 per day, then to 7,000 once CAKE reaches its Tokenomics 3.0 goal of about a 20% supply reduction.

PancakeSwap estimates LPs would have earned about $62 million more if this split had applied to 2025 volume.

Here's PancakeSwap's burn report for the week ending October 20, as published in its weekly update:

Current emissions are 22,500 per day, or 157,500 per week. That puts this week's net deflation at about 201,000 CAKE.

Now apply The Flip to the same week. The v3 and Infinity burns are mostly gone, while v2 and "Other" stay, leaving about 190,000 CAKE of weekly burn. At stage one, emissions fall to 77,000 a week, so net deflation drops to about 113,000 CAKE, a 44% decline. At stage two, emissions fall to 49,000 a week, and net deflation recovers only to about 141,000 CAKE. That's still 30% below where it is today.

The emission cut saves 108,500 CAKE a week at full rollout. But the removed v3 and Infinity burn totaled 168,600 CAKE that week. The burn being given up is larger than the emissions being saved.

The previous week tells the same story. Working backward from the week-over-week changes, the burn was about 530,000 CAKE: roughly 272,000 from v2 and 191,000 from v3. Net deflation was about 373,000. Under The Flip, it would have been about 249,000 at stage two, which is 33% lower.

There's one real offset. The non-stablecoin part of the new 12% treasury fee still funds buybacks, and PancakeSwap hasn't said how large that is. So my figures are a floor, not an exact forecast. It's also possible that higher LP payouts attract more liquidity and volume, and the team projects up to 30% more liquidity. That would increase v2 burns over time.

PancakeSwap's own estimate, based on 10 weeks of activity, is that v2 burns alone would keep CAKE net deflationary by about 190,000 CAKE a week after emissions. That's plausible, and CAKE would keep shrinking. But it's still a slower pace of deflation than what CAKE has been running at, sold under the headline of a 69% emission cut.

The final cut to 7,000 a day depends on reaching the 20% supply reduction target. CAKE supply is 329,915,408, down 11.5% from 372,837,045 in April 2025. The roughly 20% target sits near 298.3 million, which leaves about 31.6 million CAKE still to burn.

Coverage has suggested stage two could arrive about 12 months after stage one. Here's how long 31.6 million CAKE actually takes at stage-one net deflation:

Hitting the target in 12 months would require about 608,000 CAKE of net deflation every week. That's more than CAKE's gross burn in either recent week. On these numbers, stage one could stay in place for years. The "69% cut" headline is really a 51% cut for the foreseeable future.

LPs aren't the ones voting this proposal down. Voting power comes from veCAKE, which means locked CAKE, not liquidity positions. LPs are the group that stands to gain the most, with an 88% fee share.

veCAKE holders have different incentives. Today, they direct the 22,500 daily emissions through gauge voting, and an ecosystem has grown around that control. The Flip would reduce that budget to a 7,000-a-day fund managed by PancakeSwap's team. It would also cut the burn support that has been shrinking supply. For someone holding CAKE for its scarcity, The Flip gives up a definite burn today in exchange for a possible liquidity gain later.

That's why the vote is so one-sided. The people being asked to approve The Flip aren't the people it pays. If it fails on Saturday, I'd expect the next version to keep some v3 burn share. Otherwise, the emission cut doesn't do what the headline suggests.

#5395. Amazon teams up with Uber on restaurant delivery, years after shutting down its own service

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 3:00 amNovember 4, 2026 at 1:39 pm

Amazon is bringing Uber Eats inside its own app, letting U.S. Prime members order restaurant delivery without a separate Uber account and skip the delivery fee on orders of $25 or more.

The deal replaces a Prime perk with Grubhub, which Amazon made an ongoing benefit in 2024 after a one-year trial. Amazon said in a statement to GeekWire that it has ended that agreement after identifying “an opportunity to deliver an even better restaurant delivery experience.”

The new Prime benefit covers hundreds of thousands of restaurants in nearly 10,000 U.S. cities and towns, from major metros to rural communities. Orders are placed with existing Amazon logins and payment methods, on Amazon.com or in the Amazon Shopping app.

Amazon says Prime members could save more than $175 a year through the delivery fee waiver and Prime-only promotions, which it notes is more than the $139 annual cost of Prime. Service fees still apply, the company confirmed. New users get $20 off their first two orders of $25 or more within 14 days, and Prime Visa cardholders earn 5% back on Uber Eats orders through Dec. 5.

Members who already pay for Uber One, which includes $0 delivery fees, keep those benefits. But Amazon said the two memberships operate independently, and the Prime perk applies only to Uber Eats orders placed through Amazon.

The deal marks Amazon’s latest approach to restaurant delivery. The company shut down its own Amazon Restaurants service in 2019, four years after launching it in Seattle and expanding to more than 20 U.S. cities. Uber had listed Amazon as an Uber Eats competitor in its IPO filing earlier that year.

The service let Prime members order meals through its website or the Prime Now app. Amazon cut jobs on the team in early 2018, closed the London service later that year, and also shut down Daily Dish, a workplace lunch delivery service it launched in 2016.

The Uber deal is part of Amazon’s broader push to add value to Prime. In February, the company made its Alexa+ AI assistant free for U.S. Prime members. Last year it ended a program that let members share free shipping with someone outside their household.

“We’re excited to connect our restaurant community with new Prime fans, while giving Prime members a seamless way to enjoy great food from restaurants through Uber Eats,” Andrew Macdonald, Uber’s president and COO, said in a statement.

Members can share the Uber Eats benefit with one adult in their household through Amazon Family.

#5394. Series B Funding Is Up, But Fewer Deals Are Getting Done

More money, fewer rounds. That, in short, is the state of U.S. Series B startup funding in 2026, as venture capital investment continues to concentrate heavily around a handful of AI hotshots.

Crunchbase data shows that so far this year, investors have poured around $48 billion into financings around the Series B stage 1, the highest tally in years. Yet round counts are below year-ago levels and are on track for a multiyear low.

One trend driving capital concentration is a sharp decline in small and mid-sized Series B rounds.

So far this year, less than a third of deals in our sample set 2 were for under $30 million. By contrast, between 2021 and 2025, rounds in this range accounted for about half of deals, per Crunchbase data.

The smallest Series B deals have gotten particularly scarce. This year there were just 26 rounds under $10 million in our sample set.

On the flip side, really large Series B rounds are quite popular.

At least 110 companies have raised rounds of $100 million or more around this stage so far this year. That’s roughly a quarter of all deals.

Of these, the largest by far was a $12 billion round 3 for Prometheus, Jeff Bezos’ physical AI startup that launched last year.

Model developer World Labs, led by AI pioneer Fei-Fei Li, was tied for next-biggest fundraiser, closing on $1 billion in February. Nuclear energy startup Valar Atomics also secured $1 billion in Series B funding across tranches this year, with Sequoia Capital as lead investor.

For  a wider snapshot, below we put together a sample list of more of this year’s biggest U.S. Series B recipients.

Meanwhile, one of the least surprising findings from our analysis of Series B recipients is that it was a heavily AI-focused group.

So far this year, about two-thirds of Series B funding has gone to AI-focused startups, per Crunchbase data. In 2025, by comparison, about half of investment went to companies in AI categories.

AI companies were also heavily represented by round count. So far in 2026, more than half of all reported U.S. Series B deals have been for AI companies.

Overall, the numbers point to a bullish climate for Series B investment, particularly for AI startups with demonstrated traction. The environment looks particularly favorable for companies that have already raised considerable sums at Series A and seed.

Even so, these don’t look like the best of times for startups seeking smaller Series B rounds. Seems like in the current AI-driven cycle, investors are increasingly focused on big checks for high-valuation companies.

May include rounds that have characteristics of Series B financings but were not explicitly announced as Series B deals.↩

Sample included U.S. Series B rounds of $1 million or more.↩

Prometheus did not publicly announce its $12 billion funding round as a Series B, but reports from multiple sources, including an Axios post, described it as Series B.↩

#5393. XRP Targets Stripe’s $1.9 Trillion Payments Ecosystem as Ripple Integrates Privy Wallets

Ripple is expanding the XRP Ledger’s (XRPL) reach into digital payments through a partnership with Privy, the embedded wallet provider owned by Stripe.

Announced Tuesday, the integration will let developers build applications that support XRP, Ripple’s RLUSD stablecoin, and other digital assets without requiring users to manage cryptocurrency wallets independently.

Notably, the partnership could make it easier for fintech companies to incorporate blockchain-based payments into their products, potentially giving XRP greater exposure to Stripe’s payments ecosystem. Stripe reported $1.9 trillion in payment volume during 2025, a 34% increase from the previous year, according to its annual update.

However, it’s important to note that, while the integration does not mean Stripe will process payments in XRP, it could broaden the asset’s reach by making XRPL-based applications easier to develop.  Under the agreement, developers can create wallets, sign transactions, and build services using XRP, RLUSD, and other supported assets.

Privy provides ready-made wallet tools that businesses can integrate into their apps, while allowing users to export their private keys and recovery phrases.

“Privy brings proven wallet infrastructure that makes it easier for fintechs and developers to bring XRPL into real products, from payments and stablecoin experiences to emerging forms of agentic commerce.” Markus Infanger, senior vice president of RippleX at Ripple said.

The companies also plan to introduce policy controls and gas sponsorship, giving developers more control over transactions while simplifying the payment process for users.

These features could support agentic commerce, where artificial intelligence agents make payments to purchase digital services or complete tasks. Privy’s server-side wallets would allow these agents to hold and transfer funds, while support for internet native payments (x402 payments) could enable automated transactions between online services.

For businesses that prefer to avoid cryptocurrency price volatility, the integration also supports RLUSD, Ripple’s dollar-pegged stablecoin. This could allow developers to build payment applications using a stable-value digital asset rather than relying solely on XRP.

Ripple’s move comes as competing blockchain networks pursue partnerships with established financial providers.  Just last month, the Cardano Foundation joined Mastercard’s Crypto Partner Program to explore blockchain applications across payments and financial services.

Cardano has also pursued stablecoin liquidity through USDCx and institutional asset support through Fireblocks, while its participation in the x402 ecosystem targets automated payments involving AI agents.

Ripple, meanwhile, has expanded its payment partnerships through a March 2025 collaboration with Chipper Cash to support crypto-enabled cross-border payments into Africa. In November 2025, Ripple, Mastercard, WebBank, and Gemini announced a collaboration to explore RLUSD settlement for Gemini credit card transactions.

#5392. Sector Snapshot: Travel Tech Funding Heads Toward Multiyear Low Despite AI Push

Travel demand appears to be holding up, but at the same time, investor appetite for travel tech startups has cooled. Even a wave of startups promising to improve travel with AI hasn’t managed to reverse the funding slowdown, a review of Crunchbase data shows. Whether uncertainty over how AI will reshape travel planning and booking is contributing to that pullback remains an open question.

Startups in the travel tech space have raised $2.2 billion this year through the third quarter, according to Crunchbase data. The largest funding recipients span a wide range of categories including hotel management software, travel booking platforms, alternative accommodations and corporate events. The mix also includes electric aviation, travel finance and insurance, and consumer hospitality businesses, reflecting a broad definition of travel tech.

The broad trend: Investors are making far fewer bets on travel startups than immediately before and after the COVID-19 pandemic, Crunchbase data shows. This year could be the lowest since at least 2018 when it comes to dollars raised and deal count.

AI is a recurring theme among the largest funding recipients, with many using it to perform functions such as automating hospitality operations, personalizing bookings and streamlining travel planning.

The numbers: In the first three quarters of 2026, startups in the travel tech space have raised $2.2 billion globally across just 302 funding rounds, Crunchbase data shows. That’s down fairly significantly so far from the $3.7 billion raised in 2025. Deal volume is on track to fall for a third consecutive year — pointing to a market where investors are putting more money into fewer companies.

Funding and deal volume in recent years remain far below past levels. In 2021, for example, funding in the sector topped $12 billion. That’s a bit surprising considering that so much travel was halted in the midst of the COVID-19 pandemic. But even prior to the pandemic, funding and deal totals were much higher — totaling $9.4 billion across 1,277 deals in 2018 and $10.4 billion across 1,190 transactions in 2019.

Even travel industry researcher Skift noted the funding downturn in a recent newsletter, saying: “Though it’s too early to say whether this is a long-term market movement, it’s a clear sign of the times.”

Interestingly, several of the year’s largest deals involved startups headquartered outside of the United States.

The year’s largest funding recipient through the third quarter was Mews, which raised a $300 million Series D in January led by EQT Growth, with participation from Atomico, HarbourVest Partners, Kinnevik, Battery Ventures and Tiger Global Management. The Amsterdam-based hospitality software company helps hotels manage reservations, payments and operations, and says it plans to expand its use of AI agents to automate workflows. The financing valued the company at $2.5 billion.

Chinese electric aircraft developer Aerofugia raised about $144 million in February in a financing led by CITIC Securities, joined by New Alliance Capital, Vertex Ventures China and other investors. Chengdu-based Aerofugia, also backed by automaker Geely, develops electric passenger aircraft that take off and land vertically, often called flying taxis.

Montreal-based Stay22 secured a $122 million minority growth investment from Summit Partners in February. The startup uses AI to help publishers, creators and event organizers turn their audiences’ interest in travel into bookings and affiliate revenue.

Home-swapping platform Kindred announced an $85 million Series C led by Index Ventures in February. The San Francisco-based startup operates a members-only network where travelers exchange stays in one another’s homes. Its announcement also included a $40 million Series B co-led by New Enterprise Associates and Figma CEO Dylan Field, bringing the combined funding disclosed that day to $125 million.

Another large deal went to Paris-based Naboo, which announced a $70 million Series B in February led by Lightspeed Venture Partners with participation from Notion Capital, Isai and Ternel. The company uses AI to help businesses source venues, organize corporate events and manage related purchasing and payments.

Several travel startups have found buyers in 2026, including companies developing AI tools for planning and booking trips. Amadeus acquired corporate travel AI assistant SkyLink in February, while Expedia acquired AI trip-planning startup Layla in July. Both deals illustrate a trend of established travel companies buying startups to expand their AI capabilities.

Expedia also completed its acquisition of venture-backed Tiqets, a booking platform for museums, attractions and experiences, in February.

On the IPO side, a potentially prominent prospective exit fell through. Travel experiences platform Klook withdrew its planned U.S. offering in October after having filed last November.

Still, the downturn in startup funding and dearth of IPOs in the sector hasn’t affected one of the bigger now-public players in the space. Corporate travel booking and expense management platform Navan has seen its stock rise nearly 60% this year. Formerly called TripActions, it began trading on Nasdaq under NAVN in October 2025. Its stock closed at $27 on Oct. 28, up about 58% this year from its Dec. 31 closing price of $17.08. It was also 8% above its $25 IPO price, meaning much of this year’s gain recovered from losses following the listing.

WeWork co-founder Adam Neumann didn’t plan for his family’s control of WeWork to end at his death but instead expected to pass that control to future generations of Neumanns, too, says Business Insider.

The outlet reports that in a speech Neumann gave to employees in January of this year, footage of which it says it has viewed, Neumann is seen saying that WeWork isn’t “just controlled — we’re generationally controlled.” He reportedly goes on to say that while the five children he shares with wife Rebekah Neumann “don’t have to run the company,” they “do have to stay the moral compass of the company.”

According to BI, Neumann even invoked his future grandchildren, telling those gathered: “It’s important that one day, maybe in 100 years, maybe in 300 years, a great-great-granddaughter of mine will walk into that room and say, ‘Hey, you don’t know me; I actually control the place. The way you’re acting is not how we built it,’” he said.

These may sound like more outlandish proclamations from Neumann, who has a flair for the dramatic. (Talking to Fast Company earlier this year, he compared WeWork to a rare jewel, asking, “Do you know how long it takes a diamond to be created?”)

But before WeWork began coming apart at the seams, Neumann had every reason to believe that he could pass power down to his heirs.

#5390. The Week’s 10 Biggest Funding Rounds: Physical AI And Predictions Lead The Lineup

Want to keep track of the largest startup funding deals in 2026 with our curated list of $100 million-plus venture deals to U.S.-based companies? Check out The Crunchbase Megadeals Board.

This is a weekly feature that runs down the week’s Top 10 announced funding rounds in the U.S. Check out last week’s biggest funding deal roundup here.

This week featured a robust lineup of large rounds, led by manufacturing startup Re:Build, which closed on $2.1 billion, and predictions marketplace Kalshi, which picked up another $1 billion. Other sectors in which startups drew significant rounds included construction automation, biotech, batteries and enterprise AI.

1. Re:Build, $2.1B, manufacturing: Re:Build, a manufacturing startup that partners with industrial companies and innovators from the product design phase to large-scale production, secured $2.1 billion in new funding. General Catalyst and JPMorganChase led the financing for the 6-year-old, Framingham, Massachusetts-based company.

2. Kalshi, $1B, predictions marketplace: Predictions marketplace Kalshi announced a $1 billion Series G financing led by Wellington Management and Sequoia Capital. The round set a $40 billion post-money valuation for New York-based Kalshi, which says its business’ annualized trading volume now exceeds $1 trillion.

3. Bedrock Robotics, $600M, construction tech: San Francisco-based Bedrock Robotics,  a developer of autonomous systems for heavy equipment used in construction, raised $600 million in Series C funding led by CapitalG and Emergence Capital. The round brings Bedrock’s total funding to nearly $1 billion and sets a post-money valuation of $4.1 billion.

4. Dren Bio, $350M, biotech: Dren Bio, a developer of antibody therapeutics for cancer and autoimmune diseases, closed on $350 million in a new round led by Juvia Group and Lightspeed Venture Partners. The funding will support advanced trials for the San Carlos, California-based company’s blood cancer therapies.

5. Group 14 Technologies, $169M, battery tech: Woodinville, Washington-based Group 14 Technologies, a manufacturer and supplier of advanced silicon battery materials, picked up $169 million in Series D extension funding. The company also announced plans to expand into Europe with a production facility in Sagunto, Spain.

6. (tied) Firehawk Aerospace, $150M, defense tech: Firehawk Aerospace, a developer of propulsion technology, said it secured over $150 million in Series D funding at a valuation of more than $1.4 billion. Advent and Rochefort led the financing for the 7-year-old, Dallas-based company.

6. (tied) Serval, $150M, enterprise AI: Serval, a startup focused on coding agents for enterprise automation, raised $150 million in Series C funding at a $3 billion valuation. Sequoia Capital led the round for the 2-year-old, San Francisco-based company.

8. (tied) General Compute, $100M, AI infrastructure: AI cloud provider General Compute picked up $100 million in Series A funding led by Blackbird and Abstract. The company is building out its infrastructure using inference chips from Nvidia rivals Cerebras Systems, SambaNova and Positron AI.

8. (tied) Foundry Robotics, $100M, autonomous factories: Emeryville, California-based Foundry Robotics, a startup focused on building and operating autonomous factories, closed on $100 million in a Series A funding round led by Marlinspike.

8(tied) Hex Technologies, $100M, data analytics: Hex Technologies, a startup focused on building an AI-native platform for data analytics, secured $100 million in new financing. Peak XV and 137 Ventures led the round, which set a $1.2 billion valuation for the San Francisco-based company.

We tracked the largest announced rounds in the Crunchbase database that were raised by U.S.-based companies for the period of Oct. 24-30, 2026. Although most announced rounds are in the database, there may be a small time lag, as some rounds are reported late in the week.

#5388. October 22, 2019

SoftBank founder Masayoshi Son vowed tonight to “double down” on its investment in WeWork as he confirmed plans for a $9.5 billion rescue package that will provide up to $1.7 billion to WeWork cofounder Adam Neumann in exchange for cutting most ties with the company and will give SoftBank an 80 percent stake in the business. In a statement tonight in New York, SoftBank said it would “accelerate” WeWork’s path to profitability and positive free cash flow. More here in the Financial Times.

Forty-six attorneys general have joined a New York-led antitrust investigation of Facebook, officials announced this morning, raising the stakes in a sweeping bipartisan probe that could result in massive changes to the company’s business practices. The Washington Post has more here.

Limited partners or LPs  — the pension funds, the university endowments, the family offices that largely provide venture firms with their spending money — are receiving a lot of attention from venture capitalists, some of it unwanted. VCs have begun knocking down their doors with requests for fresh capital commitments so they’ll have money to invest if the market cools down.

The problem is, many of these LPs are already over-allocated. LPs traditionally invest in many asset classes, such as public equities, and they allocate a small percentage of their portfolio to venture capital. Suddenly, they’re finding they’ve forked over more than they’d intended to VCs.

There are several reasons for this situation. First, VCs are returning to them ever faster for more capital  — sometimes in less than two years’ time  — because they are in vesting at such a furious pace.

Compounding the problem, not all LPs have received returns from their VC investments that they can recycle into new venture capital allocations. In some cases, this capital is still tied up in startups that are raising much more money than in the past and staying private longer. “We have some large exposures to blue chip names where IPOs have been rumored to be coming for a long time already, and now it’s maybe 2021, maybe 2022,” says one manager who asked not to be named. In other cases where startups have gone public, falling prices have prompted VCs to hang on to their shares instead of distribute them.

The result is that LPs are having to cut back on the number of managers they can fund, and that could mean bad news for venture capitalists and startups alike. These LPs don’t have much choice. As the LP explains it, “We have a pretty structured allocation process, and we’re really trying to be creative,” she says. One venture manager who reappeared too quickly for more money was  “easy to walk away from,” says this person. “Others, we’re having to do financial backflips for them to remain strong partners.” Either way, this LP adds, “We can’t add any new relationships right now,” meaning new venture teams in particular are out of luck. “When [VCs] shorten their fundraising cycle by nine months to a year, you can only squeeze the balloon so much.”

SoftBank’s $100 billion “Vision Fund” is one big reason LPs find themselves in their current predicament. From the moment SoftBank began waving money around several years ago, it launched a vicious cycle. According to Chris Douvos, whose investment firm, Ahoy Capital, owns stakes in such venture funds as True Ventures and First Round Capital, “When Andreessen Horowitz hit the scene a decade ago, they changed the tempo of investing and everyone got more aggressive in their dealmaking as a response. Then SoftBank entered the picture in a big way, and it was like a16z on steroids.”

Blueground, a six-year-old, New York-based startup providing turnkey flexible rental apartments, has raised $50 million in Series B funding, roughly six months after raising $20 million in Series A funding. WestCap Investment Partners and Prime Ventures co-led the round. More here.

#5387. CFTC Sets December 14 Deadline to Rewrite "Actual Delivery": Where Exchanges Are Exposed

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The clock is officially ticking on the Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s (CFTC) attempt to overhaul its regulatory grip on retail digital asset trading.

While corporate press releases focused on preliminary announcements, the formal publication of Federal Register Document 2026-20888 under RIN 3038-AF80 establishes a strict deadline: public comments close on December 14, 2026.

That date anchors an urgent operational check for digital asset exchanges, custodians, and margin trading desks. While crypto media outlets like The Defiant and TFTC covered the high-level regulatory announcement, this breakdown maps the ANPRM’s exact per-question mechanics directly against the concrete exchange structures they expose. The Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM) represents the Commission’s first attempt to replace its piecemeal enforcement stances with a binding, notice-and-comment framework for "actual delivery" under Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act (CEA).

Responding by December 14 is not merely an exercise in policy debate; it requires market participants to confront the exact legal and technical mechanics where their existing architectures remain exposed.

Under Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the CEA, any leveraged, margined, or financed retail commodity transaction falls under full CFTC futures regulation unless "actual delivery" occurs within 28 days. Centralized exchanges historically operate in a regulatory gray area by executing off-chain, book-entry updates in internal databases and claiming those entries fulfilled delivery requirements.

The proposed Regulation CTX directly targets that operational model. Through the questions inside the ANPRM 2026-20888, the Commission reveals four critical vulnerabilities that exchanges must address before the comment window shuts:

In its analysis of the proposal, law firm Fenwick & West highlights that the ANPRM leaves open a crucial question regarding how the 28-day actual delivery exception applies to fully-paid transactions maintained entirely on an exchange’s internal ledger.

If an exchange's user agreement or onboarding terms contain broad margin or financing language, the CFTC signals that every transaction on the platform, even fully-paid spot trades could be swept into the CTX umbrella. Without explicit actual delivery, an exchange keeping user assets on internal book-entry databases risks having its entire spot book reclassified as an illegal, unregistered derivatives venue.

The ANPRM questions whether off-chain ledger entries can ever satisfy actual delivery without an explicit on-chain transaction. If the CFTC mandates on-chain settlement, exchanges relying on centralized databases to match order books at high speeds will face severe throughput bottlenecks and surging gas costs.

The notice probes what constitutes true "possession and control" by the buyer. The CFTC specifically asks whether a customer maintains full control if an exchange retains administrative keys, emergency pause functions, or liquidation authority. If retaining risk-management hooks breaks the delivery exception, platforms cannot claim actual delivery while maintaining centralized control over user balances.

Recognizing that instant on-chain delivery for high-frequency retail leverage is technically impractical, the Commission seeks feedback on Alternative CTX framework models. The notice asks whether leveraging registered Futures Commission Merchant (FCM) structures, strict account segregation, and proof-of-reserves audits can provide a viable compliance pathway for platforms choosing not to settle every trade on-chain.

Because this ANPRM RIN 3038-AF80 precedes a formal Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM), the CFTC is using the December 14, 2026 window to gather empirical data on how exchanges manage custody, leverage, and settlement. Platforms can review the docket materials directly via the CFTC Innovation page.

Exchanges relying on internal ledgers to offer retail products must submit technical feedback demonstrating how their custody models preserve user protection. Once the CFTC translates these questions into binding NPRM language, the legal definition of "actual delivery" will solidify, leaving non-compliant exchanges directly vulnerable to federal enforcement actions.

#5386. More Money, Fewer Checks: These 3 Charts Show The Divide Behind VC’s Record Funding Year

Startup capital is both more abundant than ever this year and yet scarcer. That contradiction has become increasingly visible in 2026 when analyzing Crunchbase data, and the trend continued through Q3.

Our data shows that despite record venture capital spending in 2026 — nearly $680 billion through Q3 — investors are writing fewer checks to seed and early-stage companies, the businesses one typically thinks of when we talk about startups.

One of the best ways to visualize this dichotomy is by looking at how much of the record global venture funding this year went to funding rounds across different tiers: less than $100 million, $100 million to just under $1 billion, and $1 billion and more.

As illustrated above, the funding surge this year is concentrated in those largest rounds, while the smaller-round market has essentially flatlined since 2023.

The massive surge in billion-dollar-plus rounds in Q1 and Q2, of course, was thanks to record-setting financings for OpenAI and Anthropic. But it’s not just those two companies concentrating capital at the top. About one-third of Q3 funding went to just 27 companies raising billion-dollar-plus rounds.

In North America, the largest startup market, deal counts have trended downward over several years, even as venture investment soared.

In Q3, reported deal counts in North America fell 16% year over year and 14% quarter over quarter, reaching the lowest quarterly total since 2023, even as North American funding dollars jumped 50% year over year to $92 billion. The contraction is concentrated in seed and early-stage deals — North American late-stage counts actually increased year over year.

Series B is a particularly stark illustration of the dollars-up-but-deals-down trend. Series B marks the stage when startups are maturing: they typically show some growth and traction but still have plenty of upside potential. But while dollars invested in U.S. startups at the Series B stage hit a multiyear high so far this year, deal count is on track to hit a multiyear low.

It’s a similar story among seed and Series A startups, with money concentrating into larger rounds even as deal count dips.

Anthropic, the biggest venture-backed private company of all, is slated to go public this month in a potential $2 trillion IPO, offering a prominent test of public investors’ appetite for the companies driving this venture boom.

A strong public-market reception could reinforce venture investors’ willingness to finance enormous AI bets, while a disappointing debut could put unicorn valuations under pressure.

But neither outcome guarantees that funding will reach a wider pool of startups. The real measure of a broader startup recovery we’ll be watching: whether deal counts start to rise alongside the dollars.

#5385. October 23, 2019

That WeWork deal could fall apart yet, suggests a new Bloomberg report that states SoftBank Group will seek approval of its bailout package with the Committee on Foreign Investment in the U.S., which has stymied SoftBank before. As the report notes: “SoftBank won approval from the panel to buy Sprint Corp. and U.K. chip designer ARM Holdings. However, the committee put conditions on its ownership of Sprint, and restricted its control of alternative-asset manager Fortress Investment Group. More recently, SoftBank was unable to fill two board seats at one of its portfolio companies, Uber Technologies, because it did not have Cfius approval.”

Tesla delivered a strong third-quarter earnings report after the bell today, posting a surprise profit and telling shareholders it’s ahead of schedule with a new factory in Shanghai. Shares rose more than 20 percent after hours. CNBC has more here.

A couple of years ago, the cofounder and CEO of a blood-testing company was publicly taken to task for implying in articles and professional profiles that he has a PhD when in reality, he’d left a prestigious graduate group three years after enrolling, without a degree.

The CEO is hardly alone in intentionally or otherwise sowing confusion around his credentials, however. Over the years, we’ve mistakenly believed that a number of founders have obtained specific college degrees based on their LinkedIn bio, only to learn offline that they enrolled for some period of time in a particular program that they didn’t complete.

It happened most recently with the cofounder of a startup who one would might surmise based on his LinkedIn profile has a master’s degree from Harvard but does not. We also misunderstood the CEO of a robotics company to have a PhD based on her LinkedIn. It was our fault; it mentioned under the credit that she’d left to start a company. But anyone scanning the site might have come to the same wrong conclusion. (We pointed this out to her team, and mention of the PhD was deleted.)

In a higher-profile case, James Damore, the fired Google engineer who authored that infamous memo about the company’s diversity practices and whose LinkedIn page cited under “Education” a “PhD, Systems Biology,” removed mention of those doctoral studies after Wired confirmed with Harvard that he was enrolled in the program but didn’t complete the doctorate.

Damore tried to defend his own LinkedIn profile, tweeting at the time, “I never told anyone I have a PhD. LinkedIn can’t distinguish between being in the PhD program and having a PhD (I forgot to update it).”

#5384. Block DOJ Settlement: Jack Dorsey’s Company Faces $764M Deal as Bitcoin Profit Plunges 50%

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Block DOJ settlement talks have reached a major turning point, with Jack Dorsey-owned payments company agreeing in principle to pay $764 million. The proposed deal would resolve a federal investigation into alleged failures in its anti-money laundering controls.

The agreement follows years of scrutiny over Block’s Cash App compliance practices. The company disclosed the development in its quarterly filing yesterday, outlining a deferred prosecution agreement with the U.S. Department of Justice.

Jack Dorsey’s Block has beaten Q3 earnings estimates, posting $3.2B in gross profit.The company has also raised its 2026 outlook, while warning that a potential DOJ settlement could be larger than expected.Strong results and a higher forecast from one of the biggest names in… pic.twitter.com/Bk0KByUDPV

The announcement arrives alongside a sharp decline in Block’s Bitcoin business. Bitcoin ecosystem gross profit plunged 50% year-over-year to $52 million during the third quarter, despite stronger overall company earnings.

The proposed Block DOJ agreement would defer prosecution for three years over allegations that the company failed to maintain an effective anti-money laundering program. The DOJ’s investigation centers on compliance requirements under the Bank Secrecy Act. Block would need to meet obligations outlined in the agreement throughout its term.

If the company fully complies, prosecutors would move to dismiss the deferred charges. However, the resolution remains subject to final agreement terms and court approval.

The proposed settlement carries a gross monetary component of approximately $964 million. Credits for previous regulatory resolutions would reduce the expected net payment to roughly $764 million. Block has already accrued $764 million for the matter as of September 30. The company warned that the final cost could exceed that amount.

The investigation dates back to 2023, when federal authorities began examining Block’s compliance practices and related disclosures. The scrutiny followed allegations raised by short seller Hindenburg Research.

Block rejected those allegations as inaccurate and misleading. Separately, New York’s financial regulator fined the company $40 million in 2025 over compliance failures.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

The Block DOJ development comes as the company’s Bitcoin business faces a sharp profitability decline. Block reported Bitcoin ecosystem gross profit of $52 million in Q3, down from $104 million a year earlier. The company attributed the decline primarily to lower fees on certain Bitcoin transactions through Cash App.

Bitcoin-related revenue reached approximately $1.8 billion during the quarter. However, the lower fees significantly reduced the amount Block retained from its Bitcoin operations.

The weakness contrasts with stronger performance across the broader business. Block reported $3.24 billion in total gross profit, up 22% year-over-year. Cash App gross profit climbed 27% to $2.07 billion. Square gross profit increased 14%, while quarterly net income rose to approximately $566 million.

Block also raised its full-year 2026 gross profit forecast to $12.63 billion, representing expected growth of roughly 22%.

Now, proposed Block DOJ settlement creates a major legal expense alongside a mixed earnings picture. Its Bitcoin business is generating less profit, even as Cash App and Square support stronger company-wide growth.

#5383. October 24, 2019

Almost. Friday. [Closes computer. Crumples.]

We’re kidding! We are tired but we’re also more excited than ever about our November 13th event, having just visited the San Francisco gallery owned by our hosts, NextWorld Capital, whose current exhibit centers on the work of the hyper-realistic French sculptor Elisabeth Daynes. (It’s jaw-dropping, trust us. Her work is also on display right now at the California Academy of Sciences.) Lucky for us it will still be there when we collectively head back next month.:)

Arcutis Biotherapeutics, a three-year-old, Westlake Village, Ca.-based clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company that wants to commercialize treatments for immune-mediated dermatological diseases and conditions, has raised $94.5 million in Series C funding. HBM Healthcare Investments led the round, joined by Vivo Capital, funds and accounts managed by BlackRock, Omega Funds, Pivotal BioVentures, and Goldman Sachs. The company’s many earlier investors also joined the round. The company has now raised $160 million altogether. The San Fernando Business Journal has more here.

Total Expert, a seven-year-old, Eden Prairie, Mn.-based marketing and customer engagement technology platform for banks, lenders and financial services, has raised $52 million in Series C funding. Georgian Partners led the round, joined by Emergence Capital and Rally Ventures. TechCrunch has more here.

Viz.ai, a three-year-old, San Francisco- and Tel Aviv, Israel-based startup that’s using artificial intelligence to more rapidly identify stroke victims in order to ensure treatment faster, has raised $50 million in Series B funding. The round was led by Greenoaks, with participation from Threshold Ventures and CRV, along with earlier investors GV and Kleiner Perkins. More here.

Ally, a two-year-old, Bellevue, Wa.-based maker of performance management software, has raised $15 million in Series B funding led by Tiger Global. Crunchbase News has more here.

Augmedix​, a seven-year-old, San Francisco-based developer of health-centric applications for Google Glass, just raised $19 million in Series B funding. Investors include Redmile Group, McKesson Ventures, DCM Ventures, and Wanxiang Healthcare Investments. Crunchbase News has more here.

AVIA, a seven-year-old, Chicago-based company that tries helping its healthcare customers navigate the threats and opportunities created by the digitization of healthcare, has raised $22 million in funding. First Trust Capital Partners led the round. More here.

Coople, a 10-year-old, Zurich, Switzerland-based on-demand staffing platform, has raised $32 million in Series C funding, including from Goldman Sachs Private Capital and One Peak Partners. Tech.eu has more here.

Grafana Labs, a five-year-old, New York-based company behind open source projects including Grafana and Loki, has raised $24 million in Series A funding. Lightspeed Venture Partners led the round, joined by Lead Edge Capital. More here.

Shipwell, a three-year-old, Austin, Tex.-based maker of supply chain management software for shippers, third-party logistics companies, and carriers, has raised $35 million in Series B funding. Georgian Partners led the round, joined by Fifth Wall, Global Founders Capital, Box Group and Aspect Ventures. The company has now raised $47 million in funding altogether. TechCrunch has more here.

Very Good Security, a four-year-old, San Francisco-based data security company, just raised $35 million in Series B funding. Goldman Sachs’ Merchant Banking Division led the round, joined by Andreessen Horowitz and Vertex Ventures US. TechCrunch has more here.

The Yes, an AI-powered shopping platform cofounded by the former COO of Stitch Fix, Julie Bornstein, has raised $30 million across two previously undisclosed rounds of funding. Its seed round was co-led by Forerunner Ventures and NEA. The Series A was led by True Ventures. TechCrunch has more here.

Foundries.io, a two-year-old, U.K.-based maker of software platforms for embedded product development, has raised $3.5 million in funding. Crane Venture Partners led the round, joined by Backed VC. More here. ​

Shiru, a months-old, San Francisco-based food tech company that wants to create protein ingredients that could be used in alternatives to cheese, yogurt, milk, and eggs has raised $3.5 million in funding led by Lux Capital. Founder Jasmin Hume was formerly the director of food chemistry at JUST, formerly known as Hampton Creek. Business Insider has more here.

Taskade, a two-year-old, New York-based collaboration tool for startup teams, has raised $5 million in seed funding from Grishin Robotics and Y Combinator. TechCrunch has more here.

Tines, a year-old, Dublin, Ireland-based startup that lets companies automate aspects of their cybersecurity, has raised $4.1 million in Series A funding led by Blossom Capital. TechCrunch has more here.

Amazon has acquired Health Navigator, a five-year-old startup that develops APIs for online health services. According to CNBC, Health Navigator will become part of Amazon Care, Amazon’s pilot healthcare service program for employees. This is the second health startup acquired by Amazon. The first was online pharmacy PillPack, purchased by the company in 2018 for slightly less than $1 billion. PillPack’s services have also been integrated into Amazon Care, which offers deliveries of prescriptions with remotely communicated treatment plans. TechCrunch has more here.

Naspers, the South African tech conglomerate, has tried to “gatecrash a merger of two of Europe’s biggest food delivery groups,” reports the Financial Times. Specifically, it has made a hostile bid for Just Eat in the U.K., which is currently planning to merge with rival Takeaway.com in an all-stock deals. Just East has already rebuffed the offer for now, but Naspers is offering cash and it’s offering a higher price, so stay tuned.

Outsourcing murder is easier said than done.

#5382. October 25, 2019

And it’s Friday! [Throws frisbee into tree.]

Before we dive into the newsletter, one more bit of great news about our upcoming event (which we promise we’ll stop talking about soon): Michael Grimes, the star tech banker from Morgan Stanley at the center of Uber’s IPO (and Facebook IPO, and Slack’s and Spotify’s), has been persuaded to come and talk about direct listings, which we’re very excited about. If you’re as confused as we are about whether these make sense for more than a couple of companies each year (current status: we don’t think they do), you won’t want to miss this rare conversation with “Wall Street’s Silicon Valley whisperer.”

Note that seats are almost gone. Giant thanks to NextWorld, the early-stage enterprise-focused firm that’s hosting all of us; to KCPR, the boutique tech PR and strategy firm; and to Carta, a platform that helps companies and VCs manage their cap tables, valuations, investments, and equity plans, for their support.

Ben Horowitz,  the co-founder of the venture firm Andreessen Horowitz, has a new book coming out this coming Monday titled “What You Do is Who You Are,” that takes a look at how to create “culture” at a company.

It’s a word that’s thrown around a lot but that’s very hard to grasp, let alone implement in a sustainable way. Horowitz learned firsthand as a CEO how elusive it can be when he took stock of his company, only to discover it was made up of “screamers who intimidated their people,” others who “neglected to give any feedback,” and at least one compulsive liar who excelled at sucking up to Horowitz and also making up stories from whole cloth.

Horowitz says creating culture was a missing part of his education, and in this new book — a follow-up to his best-selling “The Hard Thing About Hard Things” — he does his best to fill that gap for other CEOs, using his own experience, as well as lessons gleaned from historical figures Toussaint Louverture and Genghis Khan, along with Shaka Senghor, a contemporary who served time for murder and today is a criminal justice reform advocate.

It’s an instructive and novel combination, and we suggest picking up the book, especially if you love history. In the meantime, we sat down recently with Horowitz to talk about its timing and whether some of the biggest cultural blow-ups in the startup industry — Uber and WeWork — could have been avoided. These excerpts have been edited for length and clarity. Note that we’ll have more of the conversation — including Horowitz’s thoughts about dual-class shares —  for readers of Extra Crunch on Monday.

You’ve just written a book about culture that’s coming out just as a lot of questions are being raised about culture because of WeWork. What happened there?

[Cofounder Adam Neumann] had a certain kind of culture there. He had some holes — some great strengths and great holes. And sometimes that happens. When you’re really good at part of it, you can delude yourself into thinking that you’ve got everything you need when you have some massive incompleteness.

Adam is so amazing. Like, the way they got all the money and everything. And the vision was so spectacular. And everybody there believed it, and they recruited some phenomenal talent. But when you’re that optimistic, it does help to have something in the culture that says [allows] people to bring you the bad news, like, if the accounting is all over the place or what have you.

As with Uber’s Travis Kalanick, whose culture also came under fire, Neumann operated in very plain sight. He wasn’t hiding who he was or what he was spending.

Right, everybody knew how Travis was running the company. Everyone in Silicon Valley knew, let alone everyone on the board. The culture was published. You can look up Uber’s values [from that period].

Travis designed, I think, a really compelling culture, and believed in it, and published it. And the consequences of what he was missing were also super well-known. It’s only when board members think people are coming after them that [they take an interest in these things].

What are the biggest lessons in these two cases?

I obviously know more about Uber [as a Lyft investor who follows the space]. In Uber’s case, it’s a very subtle thing. Travis had a really good code. But he had a bug in it.

I think it was reported that, like, Travis encouraged bad behavior. I don’t think he did at all. I just think he didn’t make it clear that legal and ethical [considerations] were more important than competitiveness. As a result, when left to their own devices, in a distributed organization where there was a lot of distributed power, that combination had people doing things that were out of bounds.

And he was making everybody so much money. And the company was growing so fast that, for the board members, I suspect they were like, ‘As long as it’s making money, I’m not going to worry about what happens next.’

To me, the unfair part is, like, they shouldn’t get any credit at the end. Whatever you’re blaming Travis for [you should blame them, too] because they didn’t see it, either. I think that’s a charitable way of putting it.

Fountain Medical, a 12-year-old, Beijing, China-based contract research organization for pharma, has raised $62 million in Series D funding led by Goldman Sachs, with participation from Lilly Asia Ventures. More here.

IonQ, a four-year-old, College Park, Md.-based quantum computing startup, has raised $55 million in Series B funding co-led by Samsung Catalyst and Mubadala. Other investors in the round include ACME Capital, Airbus Ventures, Hewlett Packard Pathfinder, Tao Capital Partners, Correlation Ventures, A&E Investment and earlier backers Amazon, NEA, GV, and Osage University Partners. Bloomberg has more here.

Pollen, a nearly six-year-old, London-based invite-only marketplace for group experiences and events, has raised $60 million in funding led by Northzone. Other investors in the deal include Sienna Capital and earlier backers Draper Esprit, Backed, and Kindred. The WSJ has more here.

Current, a four-year-old, New York-based mobile banking app that began as a teen debit card controlled by parents and has since expanded to offer personal checking accounts, just raised $20 million in Series B funding. Investors include Wellington Management Company, Galaxy Digital, and CUNA Mutual Group. TechCrunch has more here.

DAZN, a three-year-old, London-based over-the-top subscription sports streaming service, is reportedly in the middle of raising at $500 million from investors, according to Bloomberg. DAZN is owned by billionaire Len Blavatnik and led by former ESPN President John Skipper, and the capital will “mostly likely be used to support DAZN’s expansion efforts,” says the outlet. More here.

Modern Animal, an 11-month-old, L.A.-based veterinary startup that charges a membership fee in exchange for unlimited exams and other perks like in-app prescription requests, has raised $13.5 million in seed funding. Founders Fund led the round, joined by Upfront Ventures, Susa Ventures, BAM Ventures, BoxGroup, DCM, LJ Ventures, and Wonder Ventures. More here.

Ginger, a nine-year-old, San Francisco-based behavioral health coaching app, has raised $7.5 million in funding from Health Velocity Capital. More here.

HowNow, a three-year-old, London-based workforce learning platform, has raised £2.4 million in seed funding led by Fuel Ventures. TechCrunch has more here.

Incode, a four-year-old, San Francisco-based facial recognition company designed to verify identities, has raised $10 million in seed funding from investors the company has declined to disclose. VentureBeat has more here.

Speechmatics, a 10-year-old, Cambridge, England-based developer of speech recognition software, has raised £6.35 million in Series A funding led by AlbionVC, with participation from IQ Capital. More here.

StepLadder, a four-year-old, London-based savings platform that helps users set aside a deposit on a future home, has raised £1.5 million in seed funding from the Spanish banking giant BBVA and the fintech-focused venture firm Anthemis. TechCrunch has more here.

Tonkean, a 4.5-year-old, San Francisco-based robotic automation and management platform for workflows, has raised $7.2 million in seed funding led by Foundation Capital, with participation from Magma Venture Partners and Slow Ventures. More here.

Sequoia Capital founder Don Valentine passed way at his home in Woodside, Ca., today at age 87 of natural causes. Sequoia posted a tribute to Valentine shortly afterward, calling him “one of a generation of leaders who forged Silicon Valley.”  A native of New York, Valentine majored in chemistry at Fordham University before joining Raytheon in South California, then moving north to the Bay Area to work at Fairchild Semiconductor, where over the years, Valentine began investing his own small checks into technology companies that he was meeting. According to Sequoia Capital, he soon attracted the attention of an early mutual fund group, Capital Group, which staked Valentine, allowing him to form a $3 million venture fund in 1974. Among his first bets from that pool of capital: Atari and Apple. More here.

DoorDash Tony Xu confirmed at a WSJ conference this week that DoorDash will join ride-hailing companies Lyft and Uber to spend a combined $90 million on a ballot measure focused on AB5, the new California law designed to classify independent contractors as employees. “It would have disastrous results if it’s implemented because it’s trying to impose an imperfect solution into a very big problem,” Xu told the audience. “The net impact of AB5 would be a lot of lost economic opportunity and income for the state of California.” More here.

“Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” is returning to cinemas with four previously deleted scenes included.

#5381. China’s Largest Startup Deal Ever Lifts Global Venture Funding To $59B In October

Global venture funding in October totaled $59 billion, a 45% jump from a year earlier, per Crunchbase data, in large part due to a record-setting deal for China’s DeepSeek. The company’s $15.9 billion funding round marked the largest-ever venture deal for a Chinese company ever, and came in the same month that two other frontier labs raised blockbuster Series A rounds totaling at or close to $1 billion.

The bulk of October’s venture funding was invested in the two leading countries for startup investment, with companies based in the U.S. and China raising $28 billion and $20.6 billion last month, respectively. The last time more than $20 billion was invested in China in a single month was June 2018, when Ant Group raised $14 billion in its Series C funding.

Funding concentrated in seven companies that raised billion-dollar rounds, accounting for just over 40% of October’s venture funding. These large amounts were invested in frontier labs, manufacturing, energy, semiconductors, prediction markets and spend management software. Private equity led much of this funding, along with a few multistage venture firms including Sequoia Capital, Index Ventures and Lux Capital.

DeepSeek’s $15.9 billion raise at a valuation of $90 billion marked the largest private funding by a Chinese tech company on record. The deal places DeepSeek among the Top 10 most highly funded private companies. It also makes it the second most highly valued Chinese company after ByteDance, and the third most highly valued private frontier lab after U.S. companies Anthropic and OpenAI.

DeepSeek wasn’t the only Chinese frontier lab to raise big in October. Moonshot AI, a rival open-source lab, reportedly reached a $50 billion value in October, making it the 11th most valuable private company on The Crunchbase Unicorn Board. The startup has also reportedly confidentially filed to go public on the Hong Kong stock exchange.

Massachusetts-based manufacturing startup Re:Build raised the second-largest funding deal last month, a $2.1 billion round. The company partners with industrial companies and innovators from the product design phase to large-scale production and says it has 2.4 million square feet of manufacturing capacity.

Other large rounds last month went to Axiom, which raised $2 billion for power and grid capacity build out for data centers; spend-management platform Ramp, which raised $1.85 billion and said its ARR has reached $2 billion; open-source semiconductor company Tenstorrent, which says it  raised a $1.5 billion Series E funding and recently moved its  headquarters to Silicon Valley from Canada; prediction market Kalshi, which raised a $1 billion Series E; and frontier lab Flapping Airplanes, which raised a $1 billion Series A.

A further eight companies raised rounds north of $500 million last month. They spanned industries ranging from frontier labs, robotics, legal and chips, to agentic AI and healthcare. Among the most notable was TypeSafe AI, which says it raised an $870 million Series A funding on the heels of rapid developer adoption of its decision model Jev.

A total of 66% of global funding was in AI-driven companies in October, with semiconductor companies gaining market share this past month.

The U.S. IPO market was slow in anticipation of Anthropic’s November IPO. The offering could surpass even SpaceX’s record-setting June listing that raised $85.7 billion.

On the M&A front, at least nine venture-backed companies were acquired for more than $1 billion last month, including Uber’s acquisition of 19-year-old ezCater for $2.3 billion.

With two months remaining, 2026 has already set records for acquisitions, IPOs and funding rounds across major venture markets. October extended that momentum, but also highlighted how concentrated this cycle has become: Seven companies accounted for more than 40% of global funding, while AI-driven businesses captured two-thirds.

The question heading into year-end is how widely that momentum will spread, as Anthropic prepares to list in what could be the largest IPO of all time.

The data contained in this report comes directly from Crunchbase, and is based on reported data. Data is as of Nov. 2, 2026.

Cohere is targeting a $5 billion funding that was announced in October, without reporting an initial or final close. This funding was not included in the October monthly totals.

Note that data lags are most pronounced at the earliest stages of venture activity, with seed funding amounts increasing significantly after the end of a quarter/year.

Please note that all funding values are given in U.S. dollars unless otherwise noted. Crunchbase converts foreign currencies to U.S. dollars at the prevailing spot rate from the date funding rounds, acquisitions, IPOs and other financial events are reported. Even if those events were added to Crunchbase long after the event was announced, foreign currency transactions are converted at the historic spot price.

Seed and angel consists of seed, pre-seed and angel rounds. Crunchbase also includes venture rounds of unknown series, equity crowdfunding and convertible notes at $3 million (USD or as-converted USD equivalent) or less.

Early-stage consists of Series A and Series B rounds, as well as other round types. Crunchbase includes venture rounds of unknown series, corporate venture and other rounds above $3 million, and those less than or equal to $15 million.

Late-stage consists of Series C, Series D, Series E and later-lettered venture rounds following the “Series [Letter]” naming convention. Also included are venture rounds of unknown series, corporate venture and other rounds above $15 million. Corporate rounds are only included if a company has raised an equity funding at seed through a venture series funding round.

Technology growth is a private-equity round raised by a company that has previously raised a “venture” round. (So basically, any round from the previously defined stages.)

#5380. October 28, 2019

Revolution, the investment firm cofounded 14 years ago by entrepreneur-investor Steve Case, has closed its second Rise of the Rest seed fund with $150 million in capital commitments, just like the debut fund it announced two years ago.

Rise of the Rest — which fund startups outside of the biggest U.S. tech hubs in an effort to foster innovation and momentum elsewhere — has rounded up some of the funding from institutional investors, presumably, but also from numerous very wealthy individuals.

According to Forbes, which is currently hosting a summit where Case announced the new fund, some of the new fund’s backers include Jeff Bezos of Amazon, Sara Blakely of Spanx, hedge fund manager Ray Dalio, Under Armour cofounder Kevin Plank, former Tennessee governor Bill Haslam, and Apollo Global Management cofounder Joshua Harris.

Some of these investors backed the first fund, too, including Bezos and Dalio.

Very notably, Hillbilly Elegy author J.D. Vance, who ran the first fund with Case, has stepped back, and longtime Revolution investor David Hall will manage the second fund instead.

Certainly, that first fund kept its investors busy, with stakes in 125 companies. Barely a week passes without a startup announcing some funding from the Rise of the Rest team.

ACV Auctions, a five-year-old, Buffalo, N.Y.-based online platform for franchise and used-car dealerships to buy and sell wholesale inventory through 20-minute auctions, is reportedly looking to raise $150 million in Series E funding at a post-money valuation north of $1 billion. Reuters has more here.

Weave, a seven-year-old, Lehi, Ut.-based developer of patient communications software focused on the dental and optometry market, has raised $70 million in Series D funding at a post-money valuation of $970 million. Tiger Global Management led the round, with participation from earlier backers Catalyst Investors, Bessemer Venture Partners, Crosslink Capital, Pelion Venture Partners and LeadEdge Capital. TechCrunch has more here.

1906, a two-year-old, Denver-based cannabis brand that makes a wide variety of edibles, has raised $18 million in funding led by Navy Capital. More here.

Aviatrix, a five-year-old, Palo Alto, Ca.-developer of software that allows companies to build hybrid clouds, raised $40 million in Series C funding. Earlier backer CRV led the round, joined by fellow insiders Formation 8, Ignition Partners, and Liberty Global Ventures. VentureBeat has more here.

Choco, an 18-month-old, mobile ordering platform for restaurants and their suppliers, has raised $33.5 million in Series A funding by Bessemer Venture Partners. The company has now raised $41 million to date. Other investors include Atlantic Labs, Target Global, Visionaries Club and Greyhound. TechCrunch has more here.

Duffel, a two-year-old, London-based startup that connects travel agencies with airline reservation systems, has raised $30 million in Series B funding led by Index Ventures, with participation from earlier backers Benchmark and Blossom Capital. TechCrunch has more here.

Sensely, a five-year-old, San Francisco-based chatbot that helps users navigate insurance benefits, has raised $15 million led by Aflac Corporate Ventures, with participation from NMC, Nippon Life Insurance Company, Susquehanna International Group, Sojitz Corporation, Zuelling Pharma and Silicon Valley Bank. MobiHealth News has more here.

ShiraTronics, a 10-month-old, Brooklyn Park, Mn.-based medical device company working on a migraine treatment, raised $33 million in Series A funding. USVP, Amzak Health and Strategic HealthCare Investment Partners led the round, joined by Aperture Ventures and LivaNova. American Inno has more here.

Twiga Foods, a six-year-old, Nairobi, Kenya-based B2B food distribution company, has raised $23.75 million in Series B funding led by Goldman Sachs, with participation from IFC, TLcom Capital, and Creadev. Goldman also arranged $6.25 million in debt funding. TechCrunch has more here.

Welcome to the Jungle, a five-year-old, Paris-based recruitment startup, has raised $22.3 million in fresh funding led by Gaia Capital Partners, with participation from Bpifance, XAnge, and Jean-Paul Guisset. TechCrunch has more here.

EnsureDR, a five-year-old, San Jose, Ca.-based company that makes disaster recovery readiness software, has raised $2.5 million in Series A funding led by Awz Ventures. More here.

Own Up, a 3.5-year-old, Boston-based startup that invites promises users a high-touch service if they connect with its team of online mortgage brokers, has raised $8.5 million in Series A funding. Link Ventures led the round. More here.

Young Alfred, a three-year-old, Philadelphia-based home insurance marketplace, has raised $10 million in Series A funding led by Gradient Ventures, with participation from Pear Ventures, ERA, and Newfund Capital. Insurance Business has more here. Zamna, a three-year-old, London-based company that has built a GDPR-compliant identity platform for the aviation industry (it helps airlines verify passengers’ identities before they arrive at an airport), has raised $5 million in seed funding co-led by LocalGlobe and Oxford Capital. TechCrunch has more here.

ByteDance, the seven-year-old,  $75 billion Chinese start-up that owns the short-form video app TikTok, is eyeing an IPO in Hong Kong as soon as the first quarter of next year, according to the Financial Times. As it notes, ByteDance’s valuation hit $75 billion a year ago, when it closed a $3 billion round led by SoftBank that doubled its valuation from a year earlier. An IPO would help the Japanese conglomerate at a time when many of its other investments are cratering in value. More here.
